ARMY MOVEMENTS. We have been politeiy furnished this morning with a copy of the following General Order, from the War office, by which it will be seen that several changes have been made in the military dispositions announced by us on Saturday. The direction of Col. Cutler, it will be seen, is changed from the south to Plattsburgh, where he is to assume the command, and to which place he proceeds forthwith. General Order, No. 15. Adjutant þÿGeneuaus O s ffice, ) Washington, June 1), 1838. j Brevet Brigadier General Brady will proceed, without delay, to þÿSacket s Harbor, and assume the direction of aflairs in that quarter. Colonel Cutler, 4th Infantry, will repair to Plattsburgh, and there assume the command. Lieutenant Colonel Cummings, 2d Infantry, will return to his station at Madison barracks, and Major Churchill, 3d Artillery, will repair to the frontiers of Vermont, and take post at Swanton or St. Albans, in that state. In addition to the force already ordered to Sacket's Harbor, the disposable recruits at Fort Monroe, and in the harbor of New York, will lie mustered, armed, equipped, and officered, and despatched to that post, A detachment of sixty well instructed recruits will be sent without delay from the depot at Fort Monroe, to Swanton. on the Vermont frontier, and a like detachment of sixtv recruits will be sent to Plattsburgh, from the New York depot, as soon as possible. By order of Major General Macomb. (Signed) R. JONES, Adj, Gen.

Famii.y SoiiAnrii.Es. þÿ We find in some of our London papers an account of a curious affair that lately took place among the descendants of the great Duke of Marlborough. The present Duke is a whig, and supporter of the ministry, and so is his second son Lord John Churchill His eldest son, the Marquis of Blandford, was a whig also, not long ago ; or if not a whig, a sort of non-combatant neutral ; or as we should say in this country, þÿ a man on the þÿfence. But some months ago there was a negociation for a peerage for the Marquis, which fell through ; and since that he has come out a flaming conservative. A vacancy having occurred in the representation of the borough of Woodstock, the Marquis of Blandford vt Lord JGui Churchill offered themscl ,-s as candidates þÿ the former in the conservative and the latter in the whig interest. At the polls the Marquis addressed the electors, as usual He acknowledged that it was rather unusual and unseemly for two brothers to be pitted against each oilier, but declared that the blame fell not upon birr. His brother had attempted to steal a march upon him, with characteristic whig crafti- þÿ þÿness, by causing a lie to be told his servant ; giving out that he, Lord John Churchill, had gone to Oxford on masonic business, when in fact he had hurried down to canvass for Woodstock. He declared himself a thorough going conservative, and concluded with a reasonable modicum of abuse upon the ministers and the whigs generally. Lord John Churchill then came forward

with bis speech. It .was considerably insulting to his brother the Marquis, insinuating, among other things, that the said Marquis would get drunk rather too often : and wound up with an emphatic declaration that bn was a liberal, a whig, an ultra-whig þÿ any thing but a tory. He apologised for the brevity of his discourse by informing the electors that he þÿ had got a d þÿ d bad cold þÿ!

Our readers have been informed that a j were in that city on that day. hand of pirates, under the notorious Bill Johnson, had taken up their quarters among the þÿ Thousand þÿIslands, and fears were entertained that they would make a descent upon some part of the Canada shore. By the Northern mail of this morning we have intelligence which confirms those fears. They have made a successful! landing on the Isle' of Tante, or Amherst Isiaud, about twenty miles above Kingston. The following is copied from a postscript to the Rochester Democrat of June 1 1. A report came by the Oneida on Saturday and was confirmed by the Telegraph of yes. terday that a gang of amphibious rascals, headed hv Bill þÿJohnson, committed a most þÿ daring þÿrobber on Thursday night last. The scene of outrage was on the Canadian island Tante, lying in front of Bath. Three farm houses were plundered of many valuable articles, and from all they got about seven hundred dollars in cash. One of the assailed had three fingers, as well as a large portion of his hand, shot off by the ruffians. These desperadoes have a sixteen-oared barge, mounting from 2 to 3 three pounders, and by the aid of which they are enabled to laugh to scorn all the eflorts of steamers to run them down. þÿ They can propel their boat from 12 to 14 miles an hour, and in passing among the islands they have every advantage of larger craft, though of equal speed. It will be seen by reference to Lord Durþÿham s proclamation, that a reward of one thousand pounds ($4,000) is offered for each and every of the persons engaged in the steamboat aflair, and as these and the robbers at Tante are one and the same, there is a fair prospect that some or all of them will bo brought to justice. Lower Canada. þÿ We doubt the correctness of the information conveyed in the following letter, dated Quebec, May 7. and published in the Montreal Herald. Demands of the kind described are usually made, not in personal interviews with the chief magistrate of a nation, but through the proper deplomatic channel þÿ to wit, the head of the state department. Our doubt, however, applies to the inode. The statement may be correct enough as to the matter of Col. Grey s mission. We perceive by the Baltimore papers of Tuesday that Col. Grey and his companions

The Hon. Col. Grey, 71st regiment, left this morning at ten o'clock. by steamer for Montreal, on his way to Washington. Col. Grey is the bearer of despatches from the Earl of Durham to Mr. Fox, the British min ister, relating to the destruction of the steamer Sir Robert Feel. Mr. Fox is directed to introduce Col. Grey personally to the President and he has received instructions from the governor general, to call upon Mr. an Buren for an avowal of his views on the subject of the late daring outrage, and what are the measures he intends adopting for the purpose of bringing the offenders to justice, and preserving the tranquility of the frontier. A demand will also be made for those individuals who have been already apprehended, to be given up to the British authorities.

Sir John Herscheli. þÿ We learn from the Advertiser that letters have been received in London from Sir John Herschell, at the Cape of Good Hope on the 20th of January. This learned Astronomer had completed his survey of the Southern celestial hemisphere, and intended to embark for England in the beginning of March, and his arrival was expedited in the course of May. He has made some important observations upon the star Ai go, in the constellation of the same name. This star has been regarded as ol the second magnitude, and was «o considered by Sir John 11 erschell when he observed it successively it had increased, so that at the date of his letter it exceeded in dimensions the greater part of the stars of the first magnitude, and might be compared with the Centaur , which in brilliancy is considered the fourth star of the firmament. No similar phenomenon! has been observed in the heavens, since the celebrated star of Tycho Brahe, observed from 1572 to 1574.

THE CORONATION. The following is a curtailed account of the numeration of the extraordinary embassies as far as they are as yet known ; beginning with the nearest neighbour, France. The extraordinary ambassador chosen to represent France is now well known to be Marshal Soult, Duke of Dalmatia. Austria will be represented by Prince Schwartzenburg, who will bring with him his lady, one of the most beautiful women of the Austrian empire. Russia will be represented by the Count Strogonoff, one of the greatest noblemen of that immense empire. Prussia has chosen for her representative perhaps the richest and greatest nobleman of her realms, Prince Putbus. General Count Lowenheim, lately Swedish Ambassador to Paris, will represent the King of Sweden at the coronation. Holland will send for its ambassador the General Baron Von Capellan His excellency is considered one of the most distinguished administrators in his country. Denmark will be represented by the young Prince, his Royal Highness the Duke of Holstein Gottorp, nephew of the King of that country. Wurtemburg will be represented by the Prince of Wurtemburg, to whom is united the Count Mandelsloh, the minister of that court, so nearly allied by consanguinity to the House of Brunswick. Her Majesty's uncle the King of Belgium has chosen for his ambassador the Prince de Ligne þÿ a mediatised prince, of a once sovereign house, and the grandson of the lamous Marechal Prince de Ligne, as celebrated for his wit as he was renowned for his prowess.

This prince brings with him his princess a lady born of the princely family of Lubomirsky. Spain will be represented by the Marquis de Florida Blanca, to support, in conjunction with the Chevalier D'Aguiiar. Portugal sends as extraordinary ambassador, a minister of state, the Duke de Paimella. The Marquis and Marquise de Brigniole are coming over to assist the Count de Pollon in representing Sardinia at this court. Tire King of Naples is said to intend to send new credentials to his minister at this court. The venerable Nestor of diplomacy, the Count Ludolf, will then be his Sicilian Majesty's representative during the August ceremony. The Sublime Porte sends for its first ambassador on such a mission Aimed Ferid. His excellency is said to have left Constanti-

cashmeers, and Arabian perfumes, the gallant offerings of the great Padiscbah to her Gracious Majesty. We have forgotten to mention that Countess Strongonoff' will accompany the ambassador extraordinary of Russia, and that the heir to the Russian throne will grace the coronation with his presence.
The Coronation. þÿ It has been ascertained by Sir George Smart, that accommodation can be made in Westminster Abbey for 400 vocal and mstumcntal performers, among

whom will be a number of our principal singers, females as well as males, together with the members of the three choirs. The rehearsal will take place on Tuesday, the 20th of June. A performance will be given in the Abbey on Monday, July 2d, the profits to be appropriated to charitable purposes ; the rehearsal will take place on the Saturday preceding (June 30). Sir George Smart has been applied to for conducting it.

Devotion to Study. þÿ Incessant labor þÿ intense industry has been one of these re- þÿ sults. One of the Gottinger professois, having full use of his limbs, assured me he had not left his house for thirteen years. The longest walk he took was from bis sleeping apartment to his observatory, both being under the same roof ; " all his adventures were" literally " by the fireside, and all his migrations o from the blue bed to tire brown.' Another was pointed out to me who, in addition to his public duties, had read fourteen hours a day, without intermission, from the time when he was nine years old. On his wedding day he read onlv eleven ; but, to make up for such truancy, he rose next morning three hours earlier than usual. Now ail this is absolute folly. " In vain do ye rise so early and so late take rest." Ten or twelve hours of actual intellectual exertion in the course of the twenty-four, are enough for any I man who wishes to keep the mental sap cir culating briskly through his brains. Deprived of that wholesome circulation, the brains turn mouldy ; and mouldy brains breed maggots. Iilachwood.

The Lord Mayor received the following communication from Captain Fisher, the principal harbour-master : þÿ " Gravcsend, May 28, 1838. " My Lord, þÿ I beg leave to acquaint your lordship that Colonel Pasley placed the cylinder with the powder under the wreck of the brig William, about a quarter before four o clock, and every arrangement being made, the fusee was set on fire, and at 22 minutes after four o'clock the explosion took place, carrying up planks, coals, and a column of water, as far as 1 could judge/about 100 feet high. The sight was magnificent in the extreme j not the least shock was felt on shore or afloat, and not the least damage has been done. Before lighting the fusee we had 58 feet water alongside the wreck. 1 shall return to-morrow, alter the diving bell has been down, and shall sound with Mr. Purdo, and ascertain the state of the wreck: but I have every reason to think that nothing remains below, as the remains of two masts and great quantities of plank have been picked up hy the Gravesend watermen þÿ 1 have the honor to be, my lord, your lordship's obedient humble servant. " John Fisher, " Principal Harbourmaster, Port of London." The Water Bailiff' soon afterwards waited upon the Lord Mayor with the following detailed account of the experiment : þÿ " Royal Engineer Establishment, ( 'Latham, May 28, 1838. " Sir, þÿ I have great pleasure in stating, for the information of the Lord Mayor of London, that we succeeded in fixing one of our large powder cylinders, eontaining 2500 lb. against

the western side of the brig William, this afternoon, a little after high water, when the ebb-tide had just strength enough to force the cylinder against the side of the vessel a little above the bed of the river. " The effect exceeded my expectation. A large column of water was thrown up, evidently mixed with coals, which had been the cargo of the vessel, and, on coming to the spot, we found that all or most of the lir timber floated at tiie surface, and as we found the step of a mast, and parts of the beams and deck, the naval officers who were present agree in opinion that the brig must have been blown entirely to pieces ; and if their opinion should be correct, which we shall be able to ascertain tomorrow morning by sounding, and by sending down the diving-bell at low water to examine the wreck, it will be unnecessary to fire the second cylinder which 1 bad prepared with an intention of using it against the eastern side of the brig. It appears probable that the oak timbers of the vessel being waterlogged, and having their fastenings of bolts run through them, will remain at the bottom, but as there seems reason to believe that they must be all shattered and broken to piece.-,, it will be easy to get hold of them by creeping, and pull them up, so as to clear the bed of the river of them. " If today's operation should have succeed ed in effecting the complete demolition of the brig William, I have great pleasure in acknowledging how much 1 am indebted to tlie zealous, skilful, and indefatigable exertions of

Air. Purdo, master-attendant of Chatham Dock-yard, who conducted the naval part of the operation quite to my satisfaction ; and I could not but remark tfie zeal and activity of the dock-yard riggers and of the seamen of the royal navy employed under his orders. Captain Yule and Lieutenant Hornby, and a strong detachment of Captain Yule's company of Royal Sappers and Miners, not only executed the mining part of the operation, but assisted in the naval part, under the able superintendence of Mr. Purdo. The merchanical construction of the powder cylinders, and of the lead pipes, screws, &c., and of their fitments, upon the perfection of which the success of the operation depended as much as on anything else, was executed by the master artificers of her Majesty's dock yard, under the able superintendence of Air. Howe, clerk of works of the Royal Engineer Establishment, whose zeal and ability, especially >n the mechanical department, are well knot n to the corps. þÿ I have the honour to be, bir» your most obedient humble servant, "0. W. Pai.SF.Y, " Colonel Royal Engineers." " Nathaniel Saunders, Esq." It has since been ascertained that the destruction of the vessel has been so complete that it will be unnescessary to fire the second cylinder.

STATES. !fJT In our remarks on Saturday in relation to the course pursued towards Mr. Jaudon in England, we referred to the agency in this persecution þÿ or unfriendly feelings, to use a milder term þÿ on the'part of the house of Barings, Brothers At Co., and it may he proper here to glance at the rise and progress of that firm in relation to American affairs generally, to show that the Barings have in a measure forfeited the confidence of American merchants, and that all commercial transaction? affecting the interests of this country ought to pass into othei hands. In the year 1795 or 6, William Bingham, of Philadelphia, was a Senator in Congress, and through his influence with th. elder Mr. Adams, if not with General Washington himself, he procured for his son-in-law, Mr Alexander Baring, the agency of the United States Government in its moneyed transactions with England, or rather Mr. Bingham induced the Government to change theii general Banking account from the Messrs Wil- 1 inks, at Amsterdam, given to them by John Adamsand Benjamin Eranklin, to the Barings in Condon ; and we may say that from that period until within a few years, the house of Barings, Brothers & Co , through all its changes of partners, have transacted the business, public, and private, of the U. States, together with an immense amount of mercantile business, generally for American citizens. Added to this, through the same influence, that

house was given the account of the first Bank of the United States, which expired in 1811, by the canting vote of the Vice President, George Clinton. When the new Rank of the United States was chartered, in 1816, thev again received the appointment of agent of the Bank in England, and for Europe generally : thus transacting the moneved business of those institutions and >f the General Government, and, we may add. of Hie mercantile community, for a period of more than forty years past, realizing immense commissions and profits, and at all times holding large balances of the Banks in their hands, giving them the appearance, if not the reality, of controlling a considerable part of the floating capital of the whole United States. It is reasonable to suppose that these marks of confidence gave to the partners of that house great influence in the British Empire, and also on the Continent of Europe. The elder member of the firm, Mr. Francis Baring, was made a Baronet þÿ the title lis- descended to his eldest son, Thomas Baling, who, without being a partner in the house, received with the title from Sir Francis, the mmense hereditary estates gained bv the business operations confided to that house by the American people and their institutions. The two sons of Sir Thomas Baring, Thomas and John, are now partners of the house, while the second son of old Sir Francis, Alexander, who acted as the Senior member of the house of Barings, Brothers At Go. for more than thirty years, who married Miss

Bingham of Philadelphia, and who retired from the house in 1828 with a fortune of upwards of two millions of pounds sterling, is now Lord Ashburton þÿ a peer of the Realm. He thus see that a few active young men of bumble origip from Exeter, in the county of Devonshire, have, by the influence thev possessed through the great moneyed operations

3BA5T3JR TaSJTJnTJDaSK aUBQaWJSlSTOS ATttSa of the American Government and people, not only advanced themselves to immense fortunes, but to distinguished marks of honor and favor from their Sovereign. Now let us enquire what returns this highly favored family has made for all the American bounties conferred upon it. Let it be understood that the Barings were always staunch loyalists true to their King and country þÿ and in the face of all the favors conferred on that house, never omitted an opportunity speak disparagingly to of the institutions and government of this country, and have been remarkable for their n urd of the ordinary courtesy to the citizens of the United States on visits to England, the public ministers of course excepted. The house of Baring, Brothers At Co. have never had great confidence in our public securities or enterprize þÿ they never fostered our stocks, or excited themselves to place before the community a just estimate of the vast resources of this country, or gave any character or encouragement to the early efforts of the individual States þÿ they preferred always having the balances in their favor, and the old Bank of the United States had only a credit of fifty thousand pounds, and the last Bank, with a capital of thirty-five millions had but a credit of one hundred and fifty thousand pounds, subsequently increased though not used, to three hundred thousand pounds, and then, as a mere matter of acceptance, to be placed in funds before the maturity of the bills accepted. In return for all the favors conferred on that

house by the American people, we find that when Louis Mc'Lane, then Secretary of the Treasury, drew a lull for the first instalment of the Government of France, and sold the bill to the United States Bank, which was remitted by the Bank to Messrs. Baring> Brothers & Co. for collection, the bill on presentation at Paris was refused acceptance. þÿ Mr. Edward Livingston, then our Minister at the Court of France, instantly applied to Messrs. Baring, Brothers At Co to accept the bill for the honor of the American Government, who, of course, were the drawers, which it was the duty of that house to perform as the Bankers of the United States, particularly as the heavy damages on the protested bill would thereby be saved, and which Mr. Livingston, as a man of high legal attainments, full well knew the Government would have to pay unless duly protected þÿ The Baring's peremptorily refused Mr. Livingston's application, and Messrs Hottinguer At Co. and the Rothschilds, of Paris, actually accepted the bill lor the honor of the Bank of the United State®, the endorsers on the bill, leaving the Government subject to all the damages and difficulties growing out of it, and Messrs. Baring, Brothers At Co received the cash to the credit of the United States Bank. Mr. Livingston immediately remonstrated to the American Government on the conduct, of the Barings, in thus throwing discredit on a country for which they have been for years the especial favoured Bankers. President Jackson and Mr. Mc'Lane, Secretary of the

Treasury, felt the indignity and determined to resent it in a proper manner, which was illustrated by forthwith appointing N. M. Rothschild & Co. the Bankers of the United States for Europe, who still hold that appointment and possess the confidence of the Government. This was the first step by which the house or Baring, Brothers At Co. forfeited

the confidence of Government : let us now see what their course has been in relation to their other great account, that of the United States Bank. The credit which the Bank had with that house of three hundred thousand pounds, they cut. down one half at a period when there was great pressure in this country and during the last panic þÿ they did this when the Bank was most anxious to use that credit, and thereby, as we all know, compelled thern to issue Post Notes for the benefit of our merchants at 12 months, payable in London, as a substitute for the credit. Not content with this they requested as a favour to ihern, that the United States Bank would forbear drawing for any part of the remaining one hundred and fifty thousand pounds credit which of course was deemed an entire prohibition, under the circumstances of the case, to draw for any part of that credit at þÿall. þÿ We would now ask whether Mr. Biddle could have justified himself to the stockholders of the Bank and to the public, in continuing so great and profitable an account with a house whicli bad discouraged American securities þÿ refused aid to American houses þÿ dishonored the draft drawn by the American Government and finally, at a period when aid was most needed, withdrew all facilities from the United States Bank, with its great capital and perfect security. Every citizen must approve the motive which induced Mr. Biddle to adopt the measure of establishing an agency of the Bank in London. He was aware that such agent

would be practically familiar with the credits and securities of the different þÿStates with the business operations in detail of our pro minent merchants and leading institutions of the country þÿ of the crops and products of our soil, and, short, with all the great resoui in cos of the Union, financial, manufacturing and agricultural ; he also had in view that such an agent would prove a true friend and 1 protector to American credit þÿabroad would endeavour to bring forward in bold relief the Securities and Stocks of the American Go® vernment and respective States, and have them qouted on the Stock Exchange, from which they have been heretofore entire' excluded, while the Stocks of cverv other nation on the Globe are freely bought and sold' and so published to the world. With such impressions and laudable objects, he appointed Samuel Jaudon, Esq. the Agent, who has, wc may safely say, forgotten as much of the practical details of Banking as the present house of Baring, Brothers At Co. ever knew. It was natural enough that the Bank of England, the Barings and other Bankers, foreseeing the magnitude of this agency and its important results, should endeavour to throw every obstacle within their power to the suecessful issue of Mr Jaudon's mission ; hut it is succeed i ugly unnatural and offensive to see American Bankers or Brokers uniting with the Barings and the Bank of England to defeat an object which they knew would be beneficial to the country at large. Mr. Jaudon s skill, decision, promptness <fe

great industry, together with the amj !c resource at all times within his control, have placed his agency in what may he termed smooth water, and that agency, wc do not hesitate to sa\ , every American transacting business in Europe should aid in support of its character, dignity and usefulness. We have thus shown, in this hasty record, that the house of Baring, Brothers At Go. have no further claims upon this country, nor ought to be permitted to create unfriendly feelings towards Uh Umted

States Bank, or any of our institutions; and we mention this in particular, t that house has an agent in this country, Mr. Thomas W. Ward, of Boston, charged with collecting its assets, who, in the name of that house, whether by authority or not, has been at great pains to influence the cause of our Banks on certain points. His visits to our banking institutions in Wall street þÿ his counsel and advice as to a return to specie payments, and the necessary system of curtailments, have been frequent, well known and well understood. !f wc are to have influence bearing on our institutions, we prefer American influence. and not the influence of foreign houses through agents in this country, without possessing the head or the capital of their employers.

London papers to the 5th of last month were obligingly lent us yesterday. The coronation of her Majesty continued to be a i subject of much interest, so far as the expense attending the ceremony goes. At a city meeting, held at the London coffee House, Alderman Copeland in the chair, þÿ Alderman Kelly, alter expressing his conviction that the trade of London would suffer materially if the coronation were celebrated on the scale proposed by government, proposed the following resolution: þÿ "That it v\ns highlv important that her Majesty's coronation should be observed with all the splendour usual on such occasions, alike due to the dignity of the crown of England, and the gratification of the affectionate feelings of her Ma- " jesty's subjects An amendment was moved by Mr Fearon j to the effect that a large expenditure of the public money was not essential to impart a suitable-degree of dignity to the coronation, and that the gratitude of the people of En gland was due to her Majesty arid the Ministers of the government for their wish to pro- I tcct them from a iarge outlay of their money. Several other gentlemen addressed the meeting. but on Mr Fearon's discovering that the majority of those present were in favor of the resolution, he withdrew his amendment, and the original motion was carried by acclamation. Other resolutions of a similar spirit were subsequently adopted.

One fourth of the number of individuals professing the Israelite religion in t he whole world, is to be found in Russia, there existing in that country at present, one Million 70,000. Coroner's Inquests. þÿ Horrible consequence of Intemperance. þÿ The coroner yesterday held an inquest in the 3 Avenue, on the body ol a young woman named Surah Iverwin, the circumstances of whose death exhibit an unusually melancholy and appalling picture of the frailties and sufferings of human nature. She was only 28 years old, was a married woman, and the mother of two twin children. Sh s became addicted to drinking, and on Saturday, when her husband returned home he found tier grossly intoxicated, and though nearly hi the same state himself, he thought it expedient to take her two children out of her arms, and took thein into the entry and sat down with them. After he had remained there a short time, a woman who lodged in the house passed bv the door of Ids apartment, and perceiving it filled with smoke, asked Kerwin what was the matter By this time the fumes of the liquor he drank had so destroyed his reason as to render him completely unconscious o' what was going forward, and lie jestingly query by saying,

AT'JS. "Oh! nothing; it's only n>v wife that is burning up in the room.' On hearing this, the woman rushed into the room and found that Kerwin's brutal jest was Hut too true. þÿ His unfortunate wife was lying on the floor senseless, w'ith all her clothes burned to a cinder, and her person half rousted with the fire. Medical assistance was procured, and the unfortunate woman recovered so far as to be able to speak. When questioned as to how her clothes caught fire, she at first said that her husband had thrown a lighted candle into her lap, but she subsequently contradicted herself, and said that her clothes accidentally caught fire. Before however any positive version of the matter could he obtained from her, another incident happened her which so added to her sufferings, as to prevent the possibility of her answering any question uuderstandinglv. The shock which her system had received brought on premature accouchement, and between the pains of this, and the torments of her half burned body, she was reduced to so horrible a state of agony that every one who saw her, looked forward to speedy dissolution as the most merciful dispensation which could be allotted her. The unfortunate woman lingered so until Sunday evening and then expired. As there was no evidence to show that her husband had set fire to her, the jury returned a verdict of accidental death. þÿ Juui . of Commerce.

Sir Isaac Newton. þÿ The late Dr. Stuckely, one day, by appointment, visiting Sir Isaac Newton, the servant said he was in his study. No one was permitted to disturb him there: but as it was near his dinner time, the visitor sat down to wait for him. After a while dinner was brought in ; a boiled chicken under a cover. An hour passed, and Sir Isaac did not appear. The Doctor then eat the fowl ; and covering up the empty dish, bid them dress their master another. Before that was ready, the great man came down ; he apologized for his delay, and added, "give me but leave to take my short dinner' and 1 shall be at your service ; 1 am fatigued ) and faint." Saying this, he lifted up the cover; and without any emotion, turned ! about to Stukely with a smile, "see," says he, " what we studious people are, forgot I had dined."

Watertown, June 2, 1838. Dear sir þÿ rJ he following statement relative to the scizuri and burning of the British steamboat Sir Robert Peel may be relied us correct.

On her passage up the St. Lawrence she stopped at þÿWells Island, seven miles below French Greek, about 2 þÿo clock on Wednesday morning, 30ih May 1 take in a supply ot wood. Whde she was doing this, twentyone Soine accounts say twenty þÿtwo persons. entered on board, armed and disguised, took forcible possession of her, turned the crew and passengers on shore, and after committing robbery set her on fire, and she was burnt to the water's edge There is some reason to fear that there was loss of life ; but this is not certain. All these, except one, are refugees from Ganada It is probable that a few American citizens were associated with them, but the peipetiators were mostly persons from the British provinces, and assigned as the motive for destroying the boat, the desire to retaliate lor the loss of their property in Canada. From the St. Thomas Times, June 2, GREAT FIRE AT GUADALOUPE. A supplement to the Gazette Ofpcielle, containing an account of the conflagration at M arie Gai.ante having reached us, at seven o'clock this morning, through the care of the Marine Department, we have delayed the publication of our sheet, altho' already half printed, to afford to our readers a correct statement of this sad event FIRE EX MAlilE GALANTE. A conflagration, the progress of which it was impossible to arrest, has entirely laid waste the town of Marie Galante, despite the zeal and efforts of the civil and militate authorities, of the militia, seconded by the whole population, the garrison and police. The Church, the Jail, and a few unvaluable houses only, which formed a part of the suburb, have been spared by the destructive element The Fire broke out, by accident, at an inn, at seven o'clock on the evening of the 17th of this month, and could not be overcome until next day between five and six in the morning. The country people who had hastened at the head of their workmen to the relief of the suffering inhabitants as soon as the flames had been visible, gratuitously supplied them with provision, and, in conjunction with those who occupied the houses standing in the suburb, offered them a shelter and other succours. þÿ Through the hospitalitv of Abbot Depots, who was seen during the moment of danger, at all places where his presence could bring reliet, and whose house, from its position, escaped the almost general conflagration, an

asylum was likewise afforded to the homeless victims. The losses on this occasion have been general : the chief part of the inhabitants saved nothing but the suit of clothes they had on, and a great many persons have been totally ruined. It is lamentable to record the death of the innkeeper's wife, who lost her life in consequence of her wounds, in the evening of the 10th: three children have likewise perished in the flames two of whom were the innkeeper's, who is himself so seriouslv ill, that very little hope is left of his surviving Ins multiplied misfortunes. Such is the first account of the dreadful calamity that has hurled so many beings into a crying misery ; we will not omit publishing any further details that may reach us hereafter. Marie Galantc, 19th May 1838.

MARCHING THE WAVE. " This is an age" þÿ (we beg the New York Observer's pardon ; that phrase is prohibited for a week.) " We are people" þÿ (we beg every body else's pardon ; that phrase is worse yet ) How, then, shall we begin what we have to say ? We have written so many descriptions in our day, of festivals and pageants by land and sea ; we have so often been called to paint the beauties of our noble harbor, and the gay fleets that, on gala days,

countless thousands streaming fonrth upon the Battery, swarming like bees, in masses, upon the parapet of Castle Garden, and clustering upon the roofs of houses contiguous ; we have so frequently attempted to portray those aquatic spectacles which can no where else, without the rings of Saturn, be arranged and carried through in such brilliant style as in New York, that our stock of descriptive language fails, and we have nothing that is new left to say. We were the first lo quote the spirited apostrophe to steam by Dr. Darwin þÿ since which time the beautiful passage has been kept on its travels in the newspapers, until we have sickened at the sight. þÿ Like " the tomb of the Capulets," the " all conquering arm" of steam þÿ Phoebus what a metaphor ! þÿ is constantly kept before us. þÿ So too, of Byron's poetical figure þÿ " She walks the water like a thing of life," Arc. þÿ We were the first to snatch the couplet from the book, and clap it into a regular steamboat article ; and from that day to this, throughout all the waters and newspapers of the land, our steamers have been " walking" " like things of life," until we have long since wished that Byron had never swept his lyre to such a steamboat strain. Leaving, then, all attempts to be particularly fine, we proceed in plain prose to tell how the Great Western set out yesterday to look after tfie Eastern, and how the people went to see her off. In the first place, as the people of New York seldom remember any thing but their

debts longer than a day, it is necessary to remind tliem that the day was particularly fine. The steeds of Apollo travelled their sapphire pathway in fiery splendor, while 1 band struck there was just wind enough to brace the nerves, to display the streamers of the various sorts of water-craft, and to heave up the sea in wavelets flashing in the sun-beams like liquid emeralds and gold. Of "course þÿ the government having so disposed of the business of the country that the people have little to þÿdo every body was able to turn out and see what was to be seen. And this they were the more ready to do. inasmuch as the sourness of the weather had kept them w ithin doors for a week before, and it is well for the people in this cloudy world lo look upon the sun when they can. The Great Western had been steamed round to the north end of the battery þÿ pier No. One, North River þÿ (a description, to be perfect, must be particular.) The clock, however, had struck one but once, before the people began to pour fourth in swarms that were countless, to gaze upon the spectacle. þÿ Broadway, and Greenwich street, and all the streets therewith connecting were filled with people wending to the Battery, and to the different steamers advertised to accompany the " long, low, black looking" four-masted ship with a chimney. Before two o'clock the battery was crowded so closely as to test the utility of a strong iron puling. Castle Garden was packed like a theatre on those popular nights when horses, and rope-dancers,

and " real water," usurp the dominion of Shakspcare. 1 The 1 windows of the surrounding houses were filled, and their roofs cloud-capped with people. The wood-piles at the steam boat wharves were covered, and the masts and rigging of the shipping filled w ith climbing bipeds, after the manner of the forests at the battle of the River Raisin Added to all « port therein ; we have so often written of which were twelve steamers, having on board came

from five hundred to a thousand passenger þÿeach -all destined to accompany the great stranger down to the Hook, and all decorated with flags and streamers, pendants and banners, as though another Lafayette were ul out to arrive, or the great lakes were again to tie wedded by another De Witt Clinton to the ocean. Red with animation were the cheeks of beauty, and bright the eyes that sparkled upon the living scene. For an hour before, the Great Western had been smoking like a sub-marine volcano, and hissing forth her hot breath like a chafed seaserpent. At length the hour of two arrived þÿ Hosken Captain appeared upon the wheelhouse þÿ the cry of all ashore sent hundreds tumbling upon the dock þÿ the throat of the safety-valve was shut þÿ and with a mighty heave the ship began to move þÿ slowly, at first, like an ice-berg or a kraken þÿ but gathering speed as she went, she pushed her way a short distance up the North river, when, obedient as a Cossack horse to the hit, she loomed round, and pointing her bows to ber parent-land, commenced proudly to plough her way to the ocean. Long, and loud, and hearty were the cheers from thirty thousand voices on shore. Ding-dong went the tiny bells from the fleet of steamers, which now shot birth from the wharves, and gave chase like a flock of sparrows floating m the swooping course of ihe condor. While the last preparations for ilie departure were making, the band of the Great Western struck up tire air þÿ " Behold how brightly breaks the morning The hands "

on board the other steamers played whatever they pleased. As the ship moved away, her up "Hail Columbia," which compliment was returned from some of the boats by þÿ "God save the Queen." A large party of gentlemen, and several ladies, preceded down to the lower harbor in the ship þÿ among the former of whom were His Excellency Governor Marcv, the Hon, \\ illiam 11. Seward, and other distinguished gentlemen þÿ literary, scientific, professional and editorial. From the top-mast of the ship floated a banner quartered with the (lags of England and the United þÿStates the stais of our country being blended with the cross of St George, on the dexter point, and the stripes occupying the ground of the lower sinister quarter. This union of the flags of the two countries on the same ground, w as a happy þÿconceit forming a compliment equally delicate and appropriate. 'I he sail through the harbor was an hour of glory. Nothing aquatic could have been more bcautilul than the appearance of the fleet þÿ their countless flags streaming above, like meteers in the heavens, while the waters beneath were wrought into maddened and milk-white foam by the action of the wheels. Neptune himself was believed to have retreated lo his cave in despair, since he was not seen during the day, while the tritons held fast to the shad poles to keep from being swept away, and the minnows must have been knocked into chowder. Having got well under way, the passengers ou board the Western were invited to partake ol a substantial collation spread upon

several tables in the saloon cabin, and mois toned by the choicest blown sherry and Champagne. The health of Captain Hoskcu, and success to the Great Western, proposed by Air. R. M. Blutclilord, was drunk in a bumper, whereupon the steamer Providence along side ami took oil such of the pus-

Sengcrs as chose not to visit liristol tiie present week. The steamers, however, did not take leave of their noble competitor until they had swept down the bay abreast of Mr. Gilbert Davis's luxuriant garden of Coney Island. Thev then wheeled about þÿ exchanged cheers with the passengers and crew of the ship þÿ soothed the melancholy of parting friends with þÿMusic and arrived at the city again at half past five o'clock þÿ before which hour the Great Western had crossed the threshold of Sandy Hook, and entered upon the up-heaving -an. Ami. the smaller articles of freight which the W tern carries out, is one which will he a novelty in England. It is a beautiful bouqwt of flowers, culled from Mr Thorbur ,'s -arden at flailett's Cove, and is intended lor the Quee- . It was enclosed in a tin case, hermitically sealed, with a plate glass cover, it was prepared at the suggestion of Cieut. Carpenter, and so prepared that it is hoped it will be preserved with freshness to be presented next week to the Queen, at Windsor Castle. It will be the fiist nosegay which Iter Majesty ever received from the gardens of her western neighbors. Tlius has ended the first visit of Mr John Bull in his steamers þÿ and a proud visit it has been. He has shown us specimens of his workmanship in the steaming line, vying with þÿ nay, surpassing, any machinery of the kind ever seen in this country. A single glance at this ponderous machinery, and the perfection of the workmanship, at once satisfies the

beholder of 1 s strength and safety And the rr mcnt the machinery begins to move, the op m is confirmed. Notwithstanding its pov r, not a jar is heard ; and those accus tn.ned to the clacking of the machinery of American boats, and the jarrings of every stroke, would be astonished on board the Great Western, at the silence and stillness of tiie motion. While at table yesterday, at a speed which kept ahead of our swiftest boats, the passengers supposed the ship had stopped, because of its entire stillness. In regard to the visit of these vessels, and the evidences of popular feeling which have been displayed, we look upon tlietn with far dillerent emotions than we do upon ordinary castings and celebrations The chain <>f friendship between the two nations has not only been brightened, but greatly strengthened. When two such nations as England and the United þÿStates speaking the same language þÿ having the same origin þÿ professing the same religion þÿ and having so many and such vast interests in common þÿ are brought us it were into the relations of neighborhood þÿ visiting each other once a fortnight þÿ it is scarcely possible to bring them into a state of hostility. Maintaining such relations, and hound together by so many kindred ties, we cannot goto war With each other Hence we look forward to a long career of prosperous and generous rivalship in commerce, which will elevate both nations as high as an honorable ambition can desire. if j'lu regard to the Great Western, and

all the ariuugements attending her visit and departure, too much credit cannot he awarded to her commander, and her active and accomplished agent, Mr Irvin, Complaints we know, have been made of the want o! facilities lor visiting the ship; hut the number ot visitors, without restrictions, would have been such as to cause an entire suspension of labor on hoard. In Ins speech at Bluekwell's

BAxtm vmuhwisie: mx mmmims AWM Island, Captain Hosken complimented the ladies of New York, by saying that they were altogether too much for him þÿ they had fairly beaten him ; and, conquered, he had been compelled to strike to them.

St. Croix, CHRISTIANSTED, ( THURSDA ¥) June 7, 1838. The melancholy duty devolves upon us of recording one of the most distressing, and fatally terminating accidents , which this community has witnessed for many years. þÿ The Sloop Caktb sailed yesterday forenoon on an excursion of pleasure, with a party of gentlemen on hoard for Buck þÿIsland. About three o'clock in the afternoon, the Sloop , being light, and having no cargo on board, unfortunately upset in a squall, between Buck Island and Green Quay, and her hatches being open, she immediately filled and sunk , just leaving the top o f her mast above water, and the whole party and crew were thus precipitated into the ocean, and left to struggle with the waves, and it is with feelings oj the most poignant regret that we have to add that our much esteemed fellow townsman, Brand Major Robert Smith, F. Ford, Esq. (a few months since from England), and Messrs. Adam Danielsen and George Brewer, both natives of this town, together with a coloured lad and a servant boy, there met with a watery and untimely grave, and perished in the waves ' The surtivors, William Burt, Esq owner of the Carib, Joseph Abbott, Esq. 1) B. Goold, Esq John Charles Kraiise, Esq. John G. . Krause, Esq. together with Mr Potter, and the Captain of the Carib. with 2 sailors, after being in the water about two hours, were Providentially rescued from a similar fate, and were picked up by boats sent to their reþÿlief Mr Goold was saved by clinging to the top of the mast, Messrs: Burt Abbott were supported upon one of Sloop's hatches, the

and Messrs Krause by the aid of spars were kept above water ; we understand that Mr Potter did much to support Vie Messrs. Krause by disembarrassing them of their þÿclothes On learning of the accident, the boats of the Danish Ships were immediately dispatched to the relief of the Carib, and every effort has been made to recover the bodies of the unfortunate sufferers, but hitherto, we understand, without success. We sincerely sympathize with the friends of the deceased, on the losses they have þÿexperienced that of Major Smith, from the various duties he so well performed, is both a public and a private loss, and not easily repaired by this community. We understand that most of the survivors declare that they could not have held out much longer, when they were picked up ; þÿ such was their state of exhaustion.

By a Passenger Saturday, 7th April. þÿ Our departure from Bristol was at the appointed time of sailing. Having got on board a small steamer, a twaddling little thing, we left the foot ot the Cumberland, or outer basin, at a few minutes past 2 P M.. to join the Great Western, at the mouth of the river, the Avon, þÿ not Shakspeare's þÿ a tributary to the Severn, and upon which, as some tenor twelve miles from its confluence with the parent stream, Bristol is situated. H'he day was an unpropituous one. A strong breeze, almost a gale, blew dead against us ; the clouds lowered, and a cutting rain alternated with a fitful sunshine Had our lot been cast in those good old times, w hen nature, in her freaks, revealed to grandames the mysteries of buttermilk and unhatched eggs, we had sureiv deemed it ominous, for the elements se med to Iret and fume over the commencement of our voyage. Thanks to the darkness of these latter days, however, the wind to us was but wind, and the rain but rain ; so wrapping our cloaks still closer about us to exclude both, our duckling of a steamer was p rmitted to paddle on. The scenery in the vicinity of Bristol is perhaps the finest of its charactei in England, and passing down the Avon it is seen in some of its most enchanting features For some miles below the city, the shore on cither side is a continuity ot stupendous granite rock,

sometimes attaining the height ot three hundred feet above the water mark. Starting from the stream, with but a narrow road or tovvpath at the base occasionally to relieve the abruptness, they rise, piling mass on mass and vein on vein, frowning in naked crags, the impracticable precipice þÿ or vii ling tlucr severity, gently recede, grudging their rude dills to the mountain larch. At one point on the river, the heights of Clifton were visible, with their gran ml crescents peering above like the creations of a fairy land Near to these we passed the site of the contemplated suspension bridge over the Avon. The workmen are as yet engaged only on the abutments, þÿ enormous structures, wrought upon the lull side, resembling rather the gigantic efforts of a giant race (the engrafting ot roek on rock) than the work of common men An iron bar. seven hundred <!t eighty five feet in length, stretched from summit to summit on either side, at an elevation of one hundred and seventy two feet from l<>w water mark, shows the pi ise spot, height and length, of the intended bridge. At another point our attention was attrsu tcd by me.i procuring a particular snrt of stone. It was at a little distance from the river, but at one of the moat preciptous and highest points of rock. They seemed to use nothing hut crowbars in the wotk. the part to which their attention was given l> ing .it þÿ and in the minds of many who ought to be - They stood upon small clifls almost at the top of the precipice, with ropes about their waists

and passed over the suqimit, to assist them in ascending and descending, as well as to guard against any unhappy slips, and prvirig the stone from its bed, it came down in huge masses, rattling and rebounding as it struck with the noise almost of distant thunder. Beyond this rocky section the shore breaks into finely sloped hills, abounding in wood, hedge and lawn. I uliage had riot yet burst ; still had the plough and harrow been busy, contrasting delightfully the warm and mellow earth with the verdure of the sward, alreadv in the rich hue of spring The rise and fall of the tide in the Severn is tiiirty feet, and having the flood against us, our passage was prolonged. We reached the Great Western at about 5 P. M. and strange it seemed. ,So slronglv had cariosity been excited by this vessel, that we who had now come to take our departure

It happens mostly that a very little time is sufficient to put matters in tolerable order, and oil they go, relying upon the sea to do the rest, in shaking persons as well as things into their proper places. With us, however, the derangement was a little beyond this, and the breeze having now increased to a gale, it was determined by Captain Hosken to lie by uniil the morning; so each installing tiiinsell in his little easile, found enough to do in the ai uigeiiient ol it to amuse linn lor the evening, and all, 1 believe, found an early Led made welcome by a day ol fatigue, Sunday, 8th þÿ At 8 A. Such stability, such power, si. Ii provision against every probable or barely possible contingency , and such order pi' sell ted ilselt every wliere on hoard, as was sufficient to allay all tear. That there should latterly have been a doubt as to the practicability and safety ol a passage by steam across the Atlantic, seems indeed stiange, when with any dibit of reason wo look at the question. The North Sea and the Mediterranean by the way of Gibraltar from England, have been long navigated by steam ; and it is now nearly two years since the passage to India, by the way oi the Cape ol Good Hope, has been successfully made by four or five dillerent vessels; and in all this there has surely been as much encountered as it ever likely to assail a navigation by the same means between Europe and
America. Vet, thai doubts have existed on the score of tins new attempt, extensively,

To one accustomed to the associations oi the sea, as they arc usuully presented

In his feelings, the waves and the expanse of water have in some measure taken the plat s ol friends and a stirring world ; and their ripplings and plashings are to him like the voices and glee ol boon companions, or their tossings and foamings, as the angrv discord of other elements; and the absence of these, the quietude of a calm þÿ the glare of the unruffled ocean, convey to his feelings a sense of solitude and silence not less powerful perhaps than would the wilderness itsell to one accustomed only to the jarrings and josllings of the every day world. þÿ This indeed is the only solitude the sailor knows; the only silence he truly feels ; and to see the repose of the deep thus invaded, our vessel coursing on, I can scarce call it else, for her swiftness appeared the eagerness ol hot pursuit, seemed strange as the sight of some startling apparition of active lite in the midst of the unbroken desert. From the New York commercial Advertiser May 8, 1838. A Journal or the First Voyaoe of the STEAM-SHIP GREAT WESTERN. Lieut. James Hosken, R. N., Commander. from bristol to new york. By a Passenger. Wednesday, þÿ11th. This morning we Were surprised by the appearance of a bouquet on one of our cabin tables ; hyacinths, daffodils, violets and primroses at sea! It were vain to inquire whence they came, so we scout the question, and like good heathens, receive them, rendering thanks to the Nereides. It would be difficult for the uninitiated to conceive how ardently every circumstance on shipboard is taken hold of, however trifling it may be, that can in any way be made to contribute to agreeable occupation, or even to a momentary pastime. The mind seems unwittingly to partake of the restraint upon our corporeal freedom, and to shrink instinctively from its accustomed flights to others of a narrower range ; a sail in the distance, a wearied landbird flitting by, an excursion in the boat, a gun let off, a burning barrel turned adrift, the veriest jest that can be named, trifles that at another time and in another mood would scarce cast the shadow of a gnat upon one's brain are there made the objects of delighted interest ; they are sought with the zeal of hungry childhood, and if by chance the incident, as in the present instance, assume a familiar feature of domestic life, a household seeming, it is seized with the quick avidity, and enjoyed with the zest, of a stolen pleasure. At 6 A. M. passed a large ship, showing French colors, standing to the Eastward.

At 8 A. M a brig standing to the Westward ; wind hauling to the Northward, jibbed ship and set square forsail and foretopsail. At 11 A M. an American ship to leeward, standing E. The day ends with a fine breeze from N. E.; all sail set; a large swell out of W. S W. Latitude at noon 48c ll'N. Longitude 17 10 W. Distance by log 206 miles. Barometer 30 80 Thermometer 62 Course by compass W N. W. Wind W. S. W. to N. E. Thursday, 12th. þÿ The repose last night might be compared to a tossing in a blanket ; and a dance of pot hooks and frying pans was nothing in din to the glorious clatter of the moveables that accompanied it ; to a sailor it would be quite enough to say, the widd was ' right aft,' the text to a whole chapter of horrors. The motion of a ship under sail lias sometimes been compared to the noble bearing of a stately horse ; it is a pretty simile, and a vastly exciting one when upon a smooth sea we can fancy our nag ambles well ; or even in a breeze, when mounting the waves with a ' side wind,' the exhilaration of the moment may persuade us that we prance upon the deep ; but the wind abaft' the roll, the interminable, ceaseless roll, is beyond the power of imagination to liken to any thing to which Providence ever gave a gait. The congregated infirmities of all the halt in Christendom could scarce be worse. The difference of motion by a ' side wind' and the wind abaft is, that with the former, however the ship may pitch, she is still so much inclined always þÿ pressed over by the

wind þÿ that whatever moves is sure to go to the lower side, or ' down to leeward,' and will there lie quietly. But when before the wind, the ship rolls, descending to equal points, on either side, and the consequence is, that every thing not absolutely spiked or lashed down hard and fast, plays at every oscillation to the utmost of its tether, accompanying the movement with its own peculiar music of creak, clatter, or squeak, as the case may be. Sometimes, as if by way of climax, the water tumbles in over one gunwale, swashing over the deck, and dribbling by every aperture into the cabin below þÿ then rolling again, as if to court the embraces of a sister wave, the ship descends, and again in pours a briny sheet one over the other. Sitting or standing at such a time is equally an exertion of our best powers of tenacity, and to take to one's berth may be likened to seeking refuge in the arms of a ' demented sentry box.' And with all this, the conlusion, the row among chairs, trunks, and all the locomotive paraphernalia of the cabin, the neverdying conflict of platters, spoons and dishes in the steward's room, the creaking of bulk heads, and the occasional thump and rumble of a 'fetch away' on deck, from an aggregate of ludicrous discomfiture unequalled by the most refined misery which any derangement or disorder on shore could possibly inflict. I speak now of what sometimes occurs at sea. We have not had any thing quite of this order. At noon thick weather and moderate breeze

at E. At 8 P. M. wind hauled to N. N. E. ; set fore and aft foresail, mainsail and mizen ; sea smooth, and the ship literally flying through the water. Latitude at noon, 47 17 N. Longitude, 22 51 W. Distance by log, 231 miles. Barometer, 30 80 Thermometer, 63 Course by compass, W. N. W. Wind E. S. E. to N. N. E i1 hi day, 13th. þÿ Aline morning; the sea in its richest livery a brilliant blue, studded with flowing ' white caps,' and looking gay and merry. The day has been made interesting by experiments upon our engines ; the object was to ascertain the speed of the vessel, relatively with the degree of power applied, and the required consumption of coal. The result is reducible to figures in a very small compass. The gradations were arrived at bv the ' Cramm,' a part of the engine adapted to 'cut off the stroke' as it is technically termed, to any desired proportion, which is done by its action on one of the principal valves in such a manner as patiently to close it. which by the action of the engine, most ingeniously given to it, described with a lead pencil upon paper, a parallelogram, cutting oil one corner, showing the precise vacuum in the cylinder, and by this, the proportion of power applied. To a novice, the whole process seemed a mystic operation, and reminded one of the story of an Indian, who seeing a steam en gine, fancied that a spirit lay imprisoned within the boilers, and that bv building a fire beneath them, it was excited to fury, and thus put the whole in motion. The paper and lead pencil in such hands, and the close observation of the besmutted engineers, might verily be said in our case to bear some resemblance to the intercourse of imps with an incarcerated devil. The experiments strikingly illustrate the merchnnicai principle of the difference between the ratio of power applied, and that of its result. Our sails were set during the dav i O a with the wind from the southward, but so light as could have had no appreciable influen on our experiments. The morning was thus well nigh consumed, and a day thus begun at sea, to and fro on deck þÿ upon the wing as it might be þÿ is seldom given in the end to sedentary occupations or to any pursuit more profitable than a prolonged lounge. Our strolls for the afternoon lay between the jib-boom end and the poop, watching the heaving of the sea and the motion of the vessel ; aud we were at least exhilarated, if made none the wiser by our peregrinations. The day ends with fine weather : the wind

at E. in all fore-and-aft sail. Latitude at noon, 46 56 N. Longitude, 28 17 W. Distance by log, 218 miles. Barometer, 30 75. Thermometer, 64. Course by compass, W. N. W. Wind, S E. to N. E. Saturday, 14th. þÿ The bouquet has our care. It now among the first duties of the morning to look þÿit to cull its withered leaves and replenish the water. It has become a matter of ambition with us to carry into New York a flower still fresh, though plucked in England. How incongruous it seems that a simple violet should become the testimony to a great achievement þÿ! even to beard tlie philosopher himself. f Saturday afternoon on board ship is made to bear some likeness to the termination of the same day on shore, by a likeness in its þÿduties a general clearing up and marked preparation for Sunday. We have had enough of it. Forgetting all else in the bus- " holy stoned ' ' ' Hast ever seen or heard tle, 1 will merely mention that our decks w ere holy stones?' They are of the good old family of grind stones, bearing a relationship to it, kindred to that of squeaking pigs to their grandmother. To describe them þÿ they are blocks ol stone something larger and nearly as heavy as a square 56 pounds weight. They have brush handles attached, and are used with as much sand as may be needful to aid the opeiation and bring the music to a certain pitch, to scour the decks. Now imagine a dozen or more of these put in motion over head, some two or three feet above you,

for the purpose and in the manner that 1 have named þÿ that is "holy stoning þÿsimply" infliction in the first degree, and suited to an age ere the inquisition became an exquisite. But the moment chosen invariably happens to be that at which you have just fallen into an afternoon nap, or are enjoying the raptures of delicious morning dreams ! þÿ and litis þÿ but 1 cannot find a name for the foul torture. The day being smooth, the engines were stopped at noon, for the first time on the passage, to examine the paddle wheels, and to screw up.' Lay by two hours. At 2 I'. M. proceeded. At It came up with and passed a small brig steering W . þÿ The dav throughout has been fine, with a light breeze from the southward, and smooth sea. All sail set. Latitude at noon, 46c 23' N. Longitude, 34 9 VV. Distance by log, 218 miles. Barometer, 30. 00 Thermometer, 62. Course by compass, W N. YV. Wind, S. E. Sunday 15th. þÿ Commences with a fine breeze from the southward, and a smooth sea þÿ a biilliant morning. All sail set, our ship going nobly on. No where is the influence of fine weather upon the spirits more strongly felt than at sea þÿ a bright day, a fair wind, and the sea glittering in the sun, seem spells which charm every element of happiness within us into activity and life. This seems strange in the absence of so much generally associated with our pleasures, yet it is so ; and the reason, 1 take to be is this þÿ Latitude at noon, that though deprived of much that under other circumstances might minister to feel-

ings of a grosser birth ; yet the freedom from care, and the abstraction from the world which every one at sea feels, leave us the more susceptible to a subtle influence and a high enjoyment. Sunday on board ship is mostly as marked and as perceptible by every external characteristic as it is on shore. Swept decks, clean clothes, smooth chins and no work among the crew, are as distinct from the every day complexion of a sea life, as are closed shops, smart dresses, and a quiet air, from the week day bustle of a crowded city : and with þÿ these, even the sun at sea has the same Sunday look he seems to wear when smiling upon the Sabbath of one's home. At 11 A. M. we had service in the upper-cabin. Prayers read by the captain. At 1 P. M. exchanged signals with a large American ship standing E. Day ends with a fine breeze from S. W. and an increasing sea. Latitude at noon, 45 12' N. Longitude, 39 40 W. Distance by log, 241 miles. Barometer, 30 40 Thermometer, 65 Course by compass, W. by N Wind, S. E. to S. W. Monday, 16th þÿ Morning comes and evening goes at sea as elsewhere, and every day has its chronicle. A ship is a little empire ; it has its monarch and its chief counsellors, iis patricians and plebeians, its codes and customs, its laws and their vindication, its fashions and its follies ; and the history of a voyage might be compared to the annals of an era in the existence of one of those greater members of the world's community There is this difference that while men remain suf-
ficiently unchanged at sea, to carry still the seeds of discord and disunion within, it is left to a nobler influence from without, than that of a fear of our þÿleliow-men -a dread of the

IBAWSIR TaratmrmiisK miiiwiiiimimiis AT43. elements themselves, to overcome them; an influence that in its character of an appellant to our fears, one is almost ready to believe involves the only principal of combination þÿ the only impulse to a common purpose, of which our imperfect natures are susceptible. A member of our state, of the plebeian order, was this morning given over to the chief judge, and by the judge to the king ! In plain truth, Jack had been refractory, and refusing his work, he was brought to judgment The hearing was a short one, a negociation was entered upon with the belligerent, and terms offered for his ratification þÿ either to do duty and to share the privileges and protection extended to faithful subjects, or to do nothing and share nothing appertaining to those things which men are pleased to deem wholesome and comfortable þÿ meat and drink. Jack was too much a man of the world to desire to place himself in a position so peculiar as the latter would have entailed, so accepting the former, the affair was ended. An attempt was made, on Tuesday to raise the Sloop Carih from the place where she. so unfortunately sunk, but we learn it was not attended with success In our notice of this disastrous calamity we inadvertently omitted to state , that the survivors with the exception of Mr. ( loo Id owe the preservation of their lives (under Providence) to the determined perseverance, of Mr. John Roche, manager of South gated arm estate Mr Michael Mills manager of Solitude, who. when the boat brought in Mr: Gonld alone, with the report, then generally believed, that all had perished but that gentleman ; the negroes in the boat saying they had been to the vessel could see no one else ; Mr: Roche and Mr: Mil Is forced the negroes against their will to go off again with them and search for more of the survivors, and directed the men to row a mile to Leeward of the Cakib, where they fortunately discovered Messrs: Hurt, Abbott, lvrauses, Rotter and the sailor s floating on Spars, Hatches, fyc., and brought them all safe to land in a small boat, with her gunnel to the water, thirteen in all being on board of her : and those extricated from their perilous state by Messrs: Roche and Mills had then been in the. water over an hour, after Mr: Goold had been taken off the mast. Too much praise cannot be given to our fellow townsman Mr: Arthur Rotter whose experience in nautical life, enabled him to be of great service to the survivors. In trying to secure a spar to save others, he was grasped in the. most powerful manner by one of those

who unfortunately perished, and Mr: Rotter was carried to the bottom with the dying man, Vic other not relinquishing his hold ' till death had seized upon him, and Mr: Rotter was fortunately enabled to rise to the surface, agaiu all but. drowned, the blood spouting from his mouth from the great exertion he had made. 11 e understand Mr: Rotter was very anxious to save Major Smith and helped him to a large oar, with which he appeared to support himself and to swim with strength for some, time, when suddenly the head of this much lamented gentleman was observed to fall on his breast and his face to become purple, from which it is supposed that something like apoplexy or cramp must have hastened his decease. Mr: Rotter displayed great presence of mind and courage thro' the whole of this trying scene.

From the New York commercial Advertiser May 8, 1838. A Journal of -run First Voyage of the STEWf-SHIP GREAT WESTERN. Lieut. James Hosken. R. N., Commander. FROM BRISTOL TO NEW YORK. Hi/ a Passenger. Concluded from our last. 'I iiesday , 1 7th þÿ An appropriate figure head for our ship would be, þÿ Vuiean with Neptune by the beard, an old dEolus fairly under foot. Such had been the picture had Ovid told the story of our voyage for it seems little short of a conquest of the elements. The past night and day have afforded us in some measure an opportunity of testing the powers of steam against the adverse influences of the weather þÿ a gale in our teeth, and a sea ahead, which in volume is seldom found in any part of the Atlantic beyond the limits of the banks of Newfoundland. Our ship behaved nobly. She plunged and rolled, as every vessel in similar circumstances must have done þÿ often burying her paddle wheels to the shaft, and was as uncomfortable as any huge cradle well tossed and tumbled could be ; yet her motions were easy, and her progress without intermission. In consequence of the heavy sea. the working of the engines was reduced to ten revolutions per minute, during which time it is shown by the result of the observations of the morning, that we made an average of five and a half knots per hour. The morning found our cabin in some confusion. as is usual on board ship after a rough night. Among uner mishaps, tlie little pitcher holding our bouquet, had fetched þÿaway, and the tlowcrs lay bruised and strewed ab< >ui the carpet. Our drowsy sences, after

a wakeful night, seemed little affected by the event þÿ an undisturbed nap, and an absence of care for our own proper equilibrium on a smoother sea, will doubtless leave us more alive to our loss. At 5 A. M. passed a brig lying to under close reeled main-top-sail and balance reefed trysail. At 11 A. M. on the eastern edge of the banks of Newfoundland, Exchanged signals with a large barque showing English colors, steering to the southward. At noon wind more moderate. At 6 P. M. stopped the engines, and hove to lor a cast of the lead þÿ had bottom at twentv-five fathoms l.atitude at noon. 41 10 N. Longitude, 40 21 W. Distance by log, 185 miles. Barometer, 30 30. Thermometer, 42 Course bv compass, W. N. W. Wind, N. W. Wednesday, 18th.- ft is quite clear we have no fraternity with the fishes. The porpoise þÿ the most frequent of our ocean visiters usually, whose gambols around the bows are often the subject of a moment's Merest to the voyager, comes now, dashing forward with its merry troop in all their accustomed glee, until, near our paddle wheels, they turn þÿ startled hy the plashing þÿ and dash off, tumbling and rolling, it would seem, upon each other in their haste, like a bevy of frighted children, who had become suddenly assured of having mistaken a hobgoblin for a well known friend. In making a voyage in the Great Western, every day affords occasion for the expression of astonishment at the progress of science and the attainment of human power ; nad as vain or

TasTairoaaiK mafriaaiasms atiis as common place as the question may appear, it seems to present itself there, invested with something like solemnity þÿ when and at what point shall the pile be shaken which constitutes the sublime fabrick of human knowledge ? But a few generations since, and the ocean upon which we sail, the continent to which our course is directed þÿ aye, more than half the world, were beyond the ken of man! and now þÿ what are they? þÿ what is man himself, and what are human means, wrought out by the divinity within us, compared with the creature and his aids of those days? The question, where will these things find an end ? is irresistible. At 5, P. M., smooth sea and moderate breeze from S W. At 6, P. M., a large ship to leeward, steering E. Latitude at noon, 42 58 N. Thursday, 19th. þÿ To an accustomed sailor þÿ a minion ®f the winds þÿ it is long before the novelty of a steamer at sea. with all the the attendant circumstances of its internal economy, can wear itself into familiarity. Chiefly he feels a strange relief in the absence of care about the weather or the windsþÿ sources to which he has habitually looked for a large proportion of his contentment. The never-ceasing question of the morning to which lie is used þÿ þÿ how is the wind þÿ? or þÿ how toes she head þÿ? presents itself at his waking like the remembrance of some nauseous morning does now discontinued ; and in

voyagers by a fair wind and the prospect of a fine run. or the despondency hy a foul one, and all sorts of evil fore-bodings, he hears the common parlance of every-day life, or issuing from his room, finds them distributed in groups awaiting breakfast, in the discussion of the merits of their favorite picture I The space, too, and, as far as regards the Great W estern, the splendor around continual!) surprise him. The light spars, light sails and light rigging on deck, look like light walls and great windows to an accustomed prison þÿ robbing it of half its terrors A sailor, to whom a dark cloud has ever been a thine of O watchful apprehension þÿ like a stealing, crafty þÿenemy cannot cast his eyes aloft, hut, feeling a new scnce of safety, he will turn to the squall with a grin, and, looking it in the face, bid it þÿ blow its heart þÿout. The richness below þÿ the cabin þÿ seems the expression of individual taste and the elegance of a bountiful hospitality, rather than a provision for the common participation of the wayfarer ; and this at sea too ! The change is a pleasant one ; and to the older voyager, unfamiliar as it may he, it is perhaps the more delightful, as he alone can truly estimate the change þÿ a transition from the endurances to what mav he called the luxuries or enjoyments of a sea life. Friday, 20th þÿ A thoroughly utieotnforta hie day, and decidedly a had road ; with such tracks left us to crawl over as the wind god makes when there has been heavy work. Our coach rolling and pitching abominably, to the very hubs. \ more than usually heavy sea has left us little with which to occupy ourselves to-day, beyond the care needful to maintain that position which is the pride of our nature þÿ a well poised equilibrium on both legs. The motion of the ship was greater this morning than any we had before had. Nearly calm, or the little wind there was nearly ahead, our sails were of no service, and a heavy sea, such as usually follows a ( violent gale, tossed like a floating bird upon the waves. It was satisfactory, however, as affording farther illustrations of the capabilities of the vessel. Her engines were eased, yet she continued at a speed not less than ti or 7 knots per hour. And those features in her model which, before her sailing, were the only grounds of doubt, as far as mere model was concerned þÿ her length and sharpness þÿ seemed now the characteristics best adapted to her purpose. She chares the sea upon her wafer iin<% while her bearings below are quite sufficient to give her buoyancy, almost without a plunge and a remarkable consequence of this, aided by her length, is, that her wav, though abated, as must ever occur to any vessel upon a head sea, is yet never wholly lost ; hence have we been during the whole voyage, without that jar and check, hy the stroke of the sea, to

which vessels are usually subject under similar circumstances. The nature of the propelling power has. also, an important agency in this distinction : þÿ the action of the place ot the excitement among his fellow ! paddle wheel being from the scent re of the vessel horizontally, has no effect upon h. r perpendicular motions, while that of tin mast, under a heavy press of sad. being from above, acts partially as a lover upon the hull, to make every plunge the more severe. There is another remarkable distinction in the Great þÿWestern an absence, in a gieat measure, of sensible motion or jar, from her engines. This arises as well from the strength of the vessid as from the character of the engines themselves- -a very low pressure, a short stroke, and a slow movement. loward evening the sea became more smooth ; the wind hauling to the northward. Sudden transitions of this kind, more than once upon our voyage, have led us to the idea that the power of locomotion gives us an advantage never before dreamed of; that we are enabled, in some measure, to verify the Munchausen story of keeping the rain at our horses þÿtail that, in short, we may very much decrease the endurance of foul weather, by running out of it. It would, at all events, he an interesting subject of inquiry, by a comparison of log, from time to time, with the account of other vessels, to ascertain how far the changes arising from this circumstance really do occur.
