Coronation þÿ There is a report that the coronation is to take place in August The difference in the torms and ceremonies that will be the consequence of the Kvereign being female are already beginning to be discussed, and will, no doubt, soon find employment for the officials of the þÿHeralds College. There is no doubt that these personages would render the Queen an essential, or at any rate, acceptable service, if they could, by any possibility, find a precedent for dispensing with, or at least altering, the form of the homage of the peers ; as it is, her Majesty will have to receive the kisses of six hundred elderly gentlemen on this occasion The homage is performed thus : þÿ The archbishops and bishops first, kneeling before the !Sovereign, the Archbishop of Cantebury saving aloud, and the rest of the Bishops following him, þÿ William, I Archbishop of Canterbury (and so the rest of the bishops), will be faithful and true, and faith and truth will bear, unto you our Sovereign Cord (I.ady\ and your heirs, Kings of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. And I will do, and truly acknowledge the service of the lands which I claim to hold of you, as in right of the Church, So help me þÿGod.- The archbishops and bishops then get up, and kiss the þÿSovereign left s cheek. Then the temporal peers (each class separately) follow. After the oath has been pronounced the peers rise, but still remain unbonnetted ; and each peer, accordidg to his rank and precedence,

singly ascends the throne, and touches with his hand the crown on the þÿSovereign h s ead, and kisses his or her cheek. Now, as it is not likely that many peers will be absent on so interesting an occasion as the coronation of our young Queen, lier Majesty will have to undergo a rather severe inflictiou in the chaste, salutes of the lords spiritual and temporal. þÿ Morning Herald. þÿ þÿoOo - THE SERAPH AND THE MORTAL. From the French. The theatre in Paris was crowded with a brilliant assemblage to witness the representation of a young girl celebrated for her beauty, virtue, artless innoccuce, aud extra-

ID&3T5& TjRSTISTMSX ordinary talents. The critics of that famed j metropolis had never witnessed loveliness and genius so universally acknowledged and admired. The highest ranks vied with each other in praising her charms, her wonderful skill in music þÿ the voice which nature had bestowed upon her as a precious gift corresponding with the rare grace of her person and the brilliancy of her mind. It w as w hispered abroad that she had received offers of marriage from the loftiest in wealth and rank þÿ that the choicest spirits of the age courted her society, and were spell bound by her lacinations. Royalty itself had sanctioned the general opinion. Never had Paris seen an individual whose appearance was greeted with more rapturous acclamations The opera proceeded, until the scene appeared which was to introduce ihe heroine. Long before she entered, bursts of applause broke forth in various parts of the eager and dense throng þÿ there was a moment's silence, and a creature, perfectly and exquisitely lovely, suddenly shone before them, bending with the grace of summer bud amidst the tremendous peal of the gathered thousands which burst forth and die away, and burst ibi th a gain and again till the dome trembled and the foundation seemed rent asunder Amid this tumult oi enthusiam, 1 stood with folded arms gazing at the vision, which to me seemed to have floated from the skies. A break oi music from the orchestra announced a favorite air, and she came forward to the stage lights to sing. Not in the depths of the green for-

est in the hush of noon ; not in the dark tomb itself, could reign a silence more perfect than hung over the vast multitude, þÿ it seemed as if the light and beautiful being, whose lofty plumes of snow bent down above a radient faee, was an enchantress, and by some potent speli had struck each one into a statue, with . the coloring and attitude and expression of j life. And then when the last notes, which seemed w arbled from the throat of a nightin- j gale, had passed away, the silence for a j moment continued, as if no one dared disturb the air on which yet hung the echo of the most delicious notes ever heard by mortals. I thought to myself, it fate would give such a creature to me I The iuea haunted me; I loved her; 1 was wretched. '1 hree years after 1 met her in London, þÿ Dismall! I could not believe my own eyes. þÿ There was the same face þÿ but all the glory was gone. The seraph had sunk into the mortal. It was the sun shorn of his beams, it was the angel lallen, whose brightness was I to not the same. I had just married an artless girl, whose modesty shrank from every eye but mine, who could neither dance, nor sing, nor play on any instrument It happened that wo embarked together on a voyage of some length. I had every opportunity of judging of the character of my fair enchantress. It was dreadful. 1 shuddered at the escape 1 had made. How many a man is rendered miserable by falling in love with beauty and accomplishments, instead of mind j and soul !

<0 AjS 24 From the Grenada Gazette. Cash ! Cash ! for this we strive and toil From morning until night, Some plough the sea and some the soil ; Some practice Cook, and others Hoyle- On politics some write : And all who wish to cut a dash Must have thnr pockets crammed with cash,

I offer my service, sir, And my good wishes þÿtoo Pray how much are you worth a year l Your pocket is too short, I fear, To help my projects through . If so your service is but trash : But I'm your man if you have cash. þÿ

Behold those interesting girls, Who smite divinely sweet ; Quite good enough for lords or earls ; Whose snowy teeth and raven curls Are very hard to þÿbeat Indeed, the sweetest girls on earth þÿ Pray tell me how much cash they're worth.

And love is bargain'd for and sold, By rules precise and. narrow ? Changed from the god he was of old, His quiver is of burnished gold, And silver every þÿarrow And now whene'er he bends his bow He's apt to lay a fortune low.

For Cash we sail the ocean o'er, And many a distant þÿsea The want of Cash condemns the poor And Cash unbars the prison door, And sets the convict free-' Stronger than learning oj the schools, The destiny of earth, Cash rules.

Without it, man but badly fares In all terrestrial things ; And when a while he bravely bears Lift's tempests, and its load of cares, And writhes beneath its þÿstings Down to where Cash exerts no power, He sinks like a neglected flower.

Letter of the Emperor Joseph 2d to General Falkenstine: Translated from the German for the Christian Statesman. the Count of de K General: You will immediately arrest þÿ and Captain þÿV . The Count is young, passionate, and ii fluenced by wrong notions of birth, and a false sense of honor. Capt. W is an old soldier, who has a mania for adjusting ev ry dispute with the sword and pistol, and who has received the challenge of the young Count with a warmth ill becoming bis graver years. I will suffer no duelling in mv army. I despise the principle of those who attempt to justify the practice, and who think there is any heroism in the murderous practice of running one another through the body in cold blood. When I have officers who bravely expose themselves to every danger in facing the enemies of their country, and who at all times exhibit courage and resolution in attack and defence, they have my esteem and respeet ; the coolness with which they they can meet death in the service of their country, redounds highly to their honor, and will entitle them to live in the grateful memory of their countrymen But where men are to be found ready on the slightest cause, to sacrifice every thing to their hatred, vengeance, or a point of false honor, 1 cannot but despise them ; in my eyes they are no better than the Roman gladiators of old. Order a courtmartial to try these two officers ; investigate the subject of their dispute with the impartiality which justice demands ; and he who is

guilty, let him be a sacrifice to the offended laws. This practice of duelling is a barbarous custom worthy only of the age of the Tamerlanes and Bajazetts, and a disgrace to our enlightened age and country. Do but think of the melancholy effects which it produces in private life, in the bosom of families, in hearts which nature has not made hardy enough to bear such losses 1 will have it suppressed and punished even if it should deprive me of half of my officers ! There will be men enough left for the maintenance of the good causes þÿ men who now to unite the character of the hero with that of the good subject and the honest citizen ; and these only are such as are actuated by a due regard to the laws of their country, and a proper respect for the feelings of the good and upright. JOSEPH.

A writer, who says he was sixteen years a prisoner for the crime of debt, in the city of New York, has the following paragraph in illustration of this barbarous system: þÿ It is a tiorrid place þÿ and many a time, when through the grates of my prison window, I have watched the last rays of the sitting sun as they gilded some neighboring spire, 1 have wondered that any man could find it in his heart to put a fellow being in jail for debt. I have at leasi given up the hopes of Liberty þÿ blessed Liberty I I can hardly write the wo 1 without dropping tear at the recollection of the joyous days of Liberty which are gone forever. 1 am sad when I think how they have fled away like a dream, and that neither I, nor my creditors can ever recall them. When 1 entered the walls of this terrible jail, in which, amid die rattling of chains, I am writing this litiie story of my life, I was young, in good health, blest with a wife whom 1 adored, and as tine a boy as ever smiled in the face of a father. (From the Barbadian April, 14, 1838.) A Buried City Discovered in Peru. The Captain of an Ameiican vessel, named Ray, has lately discovered on the coast of Peru, in the environs of Garvey, province of Fruscillo, an ancient buried city of considerable extent. Following the course ol some excavations which he made, he found the walls of the edifices still standing, and many of them in a complete state of preservation. He infers from the numbers and extent of them that the population of the city could not have been less than 3,000 souls. Great numbers of skeletons and mummies in a perfect state of preservation were found among the private and sacred edifices, and a great number of domestic utensils, articles of furniture,

coins, and curious antiquities. The earthquake by which it would appear the city was engulphed appears to have surprised the inhabitants like those of Pompeii, in the midst ol their daily avocations, and many of them were found by Captain Ray singularly preserved, by the exclusion of atmospheric air in the precise action or employment of the moment when overwhelmed. One man, standing up as if in the act of escaping, was dressed in a light robe, in the folds of which coins were found, which have been sent to the scientific institution of Lima for investigation. A female was also found sitting in a chair before a loom, which contained an unfinished piece of cotton-stuff, which she was in the act of weaving The cotton-stuff (which is of a gaudy pattern, but very neatly fabricated) is about eight inches in diameter, and appears have been only half completed. to A great number of antiquities and curiosities, found in this American Herculaneum grave have been sent to the museum of Lima þÿ Constitutional.

My Dear Sir. þÿ X propose to say a few words on the question whether the Sanies should resume specie payments in May next. 1 do this because my position seems to justify if not require it. For nineteen years I have been connected with the Institution which caused the Inst resumption, and during ail that period my efforts have been directed to secure to the country the benefits of a sound currency, and to banish from circulation eve. ry thing but the precious metals and notes always Convertible into them. 1 think that no other currency is safe or tolerable $ and that we should now return to it at the first moment it can be done permanently. For this purpose the institution to which 1 belong has made great efforts. Since the suspension in May last it has bought and added to its vaults nearly three mtllions of dollars in gold and silver \ and now with a capital of at first a passing outcry, has settled trite an thirty-five millions, its notes in circulation are six millions, while its specie, after paying more than half a million to the Government of the United States, amounts to -early four millions, and it has eight or ten millions in funds in Europe. Our priciples therefore incline us to an early resumption our preparations would justify it þÿ and if we were at all influenced b v the poor ambition of doing what others cannot do so readily, or the still poorer desire of profilting by the disasters of others,

the occasion would certainly be tempting. þÿ But the Bank of the United Stales makes common cause with the other Banks, and the character and prosperity of the country are identified with its banking system. They must stand or fall together þÿ and it is of vital importance that the banks should act wisely and act harmoniously, and above all that they should not suffer themselves to be driven, by the dread of being thought weak, into rash and hazardous enterprizes The great prerogative .strength of is not to be afraid of doing right i and it belongs those who have to no fear that prudent counsels will be mistaken for timidity, to examine calmly whether the general interests of the country rccomtr, nd the voluntary resumption of specie payments in May next. The suspension found us with a heavy debt to the Ranks þÿ not less probably than 500 millions þÿ with large balances front the Southern and Western States to the Atlantic cities, and with a Very considerable debt to Europe, þÿ All parties were willing to pay ; almost all were able to pay ; but great forbearance and great indulgence were necessary from the creditor, and above all, after such a convulsion, the great restorer was time to settle ; time to adjust their accounts ; time to send the debtors' crops to market ; time to dispose of his property with the least sacrifice ; time to bring out his resources to pay his þÿdebts. before the suspension, finds his ability to pro- In all the large movements of human affairs, as in the operations of nature, the great law is gentleness þÿ violence is the last resource of weakness. The disease of the country was an overstrained and distempered energy þÿ The remedy was repose. The question of the currency, though important, was only secondary. The first care was to pay our debts, and especially not to depreciate the value of our means of paying them. Accordingly it seemed to me that after the suspen-

sion, the true course of this country was to begin a gentle and gradual diminution of loans sufficient to prevent the hazards of expansion while the restraints of specie payments was removed, and to prepare for their resumption, but wiih no rash connection as to the amount which the several banks could curtail þÿ to make no violent changes in the standard of value, and give time for a settlement with foreigners, and among ourselves, on the same or nearly the same basis upon which these mutual engagements were contracted þÿ letting the crops go to their destined markets without depreciating their prices. þÿ After this, the resumption, with the aid of Congress would have been easy and spontaneous. It was in this spirit tliat tbe Bank of loc United States has not diminished ten per cent, of its loans while it added about three þÿ millions to its specie þÿ and wiil have given the necessary facilities for shipping the crops of the South and West to the amount of probably fifteen or twenty millions of dollars; placing its own confidential agent in England to protect the great and pecuniary interests of the country. This seemed to be its proper function. It was thus that it hoped to discharge duty its to the whole Union. It was thus, too, it could show its fidelity to Pennsylvania, by aiding public improvements by its þÿ keeping its business and its people in comparative ease, and by not suffering the prosperity of its commercial capital to Do prostrated þÿ objects these, far more important than

whether specie payments be resumed a few months sooner or later. The injurious effects of a contrary course are seen in all the relations of business Take for instance the debts to the Banks and to individuals. The debts were mainly contract cu when the currency was abundant They must now be paid in a very altered state of the þÿcurrency and it is necessary to proceed

JBA3T3E TasTiwa>3sx þÿBa«aa» Jt»©3 a'tsswith extreme caution when the relation of the debtor to his creditor is changed by events which neither could control, because if this change be not made very gradually so as to bring at the same time all the other relations of life to the same standard, you inflict injustice or perhaps ruin on the debtor. It was thus that England continued the suspension for twenty-five years and by act of Parliament gave several vehrs notice of the progressive resumption in order that all the business of the country should adjust itself to the approaching change. Of the effect of any sudden movement, we have before us a striking instance. It appears by the published statements of the Ranks of the city ot New York, that since the suspension to March 1, 1838, they have reduced their loans and discounts from forty-six millions to thirty millions and their circulation from nine millions to two millions þÿ an aggregate diminution from fifty-five millions to thirty-three millions, if this, or any thing near this, be the reduction, what is the consequence 7 A man who contracted a debt to the Ranks in New ) ork,

vide means for the payment of that debt reduced one third or nearly one half- þÿ say, the dollar he now pays is equivalent to one and a half or almost two dollars when he borrowed it, besides the interest. Such a j process of reduction would have been wholly intolerable, if the citizens had not escaped from it and sought alleviation by loans elsewhere. But if the other cities had followed i suspending, and entirely approved of it as the the example of New York and made simi'ia) reductions, the whole country would have sunk under it or revolted against it. These inequalities between members of the same community became more striking when applied to engagements between distant parts of the Union. The Atlantic cities, for instance, were creditors of the Southern and W estern States for goods sold to them, to be paid lor either in those States, or in the Atlantic cities þÿ their currency being so nearly the same that the exchange would not cost as much as the mere transportation of the specie. When the day of payment arrives, the creditor city suddenly makes an artificial scarcity of its own currency þÿ renders the only money it will receive in payment almost inaccessible to its debtor þÿ reducing at the same time the rates of exchange, and the prices of every thing. This rigor instantly recoils on the creditor. If payment is made in the Southern and Western States, the Atlantic merchant losses the whole depreciation in the exchange. þÿ If payment is to be made in the At-

lantic cities, and the debtor sends produce to pay his debt, the scarcity of money obliges him to sacrifice it þÿ il lie sends the Bank notes of his country they sink to seventy-five per cent in value þÿ and he losses (he difference. þÿ If lie brings the stock of his State, the scarcity ol money renders their negociution impossible. Once disappointed in this way, he sends no more produce no more Bank notes þÿ þÿ and the creditors, in turn suffer more than the difference by the delay. So in respect to foreigners. We owe a large debt to France and England. Why should we destroy the value of our only means of paying it 7 We can pay it only in cask, or produce, or stocks. As to cash this þÿ debt was contracted in an abundant currency. By this artificial scarcity of money we arc obliged pay to it in a currency more valuable by one half or one third. Even at that rate we can neither borrow the money, nor raise

it by sales except by ruinous sacrifice. We then may pay it in produce, ui in stocks, but the same scarcity sinks tiie value of both. A debt contracted when cotton was at twenty cents, we have to pay when cotton is ten cents a pound. If we propose to pay in stocks, these too have sunk perhaps twentyfive per cent, on their price last year, (fur resources then are diminished in value while our debt, is increasing by interest. The consequence is that the foreign debt is postponed. This operates injuriously to both parties þÿ to the domestic debtor by reducing his means of payment þÿ to the foreign creditor by the delay & the hazard of his debt. It is true if he could now receive his money he would remit it home at a low rate. But then the same scarcity which lowers the rate of remittance, prevents his receiving any tiling to remit þÿ and so tar from being interesied in the early resumption, it injures him essentially, because the forced preparation for it by crushing the resources of his debtors renders them alike unable and unwilling to pay. What the foreign creditor wants is payment þÿ payment of tiie debt, not in a better currency, but in an equal currency or if necessary, in an infethat is to j rior currency, because lie can better support a high rate of remittance than a reduced or postponed payment. There prevails a notion that the credit of the country abroad will be injured by not resuming. Not in the least. Every body connected with America knew the reason of

only measure that could have saved the country. What Europeans want now is that wc should pay our debts. That is our first duty, and it they sec, as tiie v cannot fail to see that these premature efforts to resume specie payments prevent the collection of what is due to them, they will perceive, that in endeavoring to secure an object wholly domestic, they have been sacrificed. In respect to the dividends and the stock, payable abroad, many ot them are payable in pounds sterling, or guilders, or francs, so that we place tiie money there at our ow n cost þÿ and as to divi- (lends payable here, they have almost universally been remitted in the equivalents to specie. What the general merchants of France oi England desire, is that vve should take their merchandize þÿ that we should trade wiih them. The state of om currency is a very subordinate concern. You deal wiih them and pay them in their own currency. They know little and care less about the sort of currency in which you deal with the South and West. Resides, who are to reproach us with the depreciation of our notes. The English? But the Bank of England suspended specie payments for twenty -five years during nearly all which time every American Bank paid specie, and men in England were forced by law to take the notes of the Bank of England when they were at thirty per cent disþÿcount whereas no mail is obliged here lo take any note of anv Bank-- and at ibis moment a paper dollar in Rhikulclpliia or New York, will buy a silver dollar delivered in

London. The question then of the resumption is one exclusively domestic- one which, however important at home, docs not effect the credit of the country abroad. VI. Wc come now to the question whether if an early resumption he practicable, the month of May is a lit time. ,\1\ impression is that the month of Mav is a vci \ unfit time, The resumption, to he useful, must ho general; and no arrangement can be satislac-'

BAirafc torv which does not include the Southern and Southwestern States. These I do not think are vet ready to resume. They are straining everv nerve to pay their debts Their crops are going forward to provide funds in Europe and at the North þÿ the Banks are laboring to meet their notes at the Nortli þÿ the Legislatures are pledging their credit to raise funds in order that their people may pay their debts. Why should we repulse them t þÿ Ail they want is time. They have not yet had the benefit of a single crop, and they may require another ; and instead of discrediting them, or diminishing the value of their produce, or curtailing their facilities in sending their crops to market, it better help is' to them and wait till they are more advanced in their preparations. The employment of credit, either of Banks or of individuals most useful to the country at this moment, is to forward its produce to Europe. Instead of this the Banks arc reducing these facilities, and calling upon their debtors for payment. þÿ Ibis seems very unreasonable. It is stopping the locomotives as they are carrying the crop to market. The month of May too is not the light time of the year. For example, it requires on an average about fifty days to take cotum from New Orleans to Liverpool. Supposing it immediately sold, the usage is at the end of ten days to give a banker's acceptance, payable in two months, so that by the month of May there would not be actually realized more than the cotton which left New

Orleans before January, when no more than one fourth or one fifth of the whole crop had been shipped. Much, ol course, is drawn for when shipped, hut I speak now of the actual obtaining possession of tiic proceeds of the crop, and at all events not one half of the crop will have reached Europe by the month ot May. The Spring is moreover, the season when the credits given for the shipments of Southern and Western produce, are maturing at the North ; and the crop from which reimbursements are to come remain unsold in Europe. The Spring too, is the time when the Western business has brought from the interior the notes of the Atlantic Banks, when the circulation presses more upon them than at any other period, and when specie is. wanted for the trade to China and India, making that time particularly unpropitious for the resumption. VII. It remains now to inquire how far these general views of the expediency of the resumption in May should he changed by the determination of the Banks of the city of New York to resume at that period. For the gentlemen of New York who announce that decision, 1 have great personal respect, and under ordinary circumstances would willingly yield my own convictions to their better opportunities and understanding. But the natural influence of their judgment is weakened by the knowledge of the fact, that he Banks of New York would not have had the least idea of a resumption in May þÿ but because the inmunily allowed by the Legislature will then expire, and they tear that it will not

he renewed. This was distinctly avowed at the Bank C'onventiop, and the deputation who visited Philadelphia repeated it again and again. Now this mn v be a very good reason for the Banks of New York to resume þÿ but certainly no reason whatever for the Banks of Pennsylvania to do tbe same. The Stales of of purchasers. You make an artificial scarci- Pennsylvania, of V irginia, of Kentucky, have Legislatures us well ns New York has, and they have refused to direct their bank to re

Tjrrnrm$TL mcmotmi þÿwm < m af x - fiamms . m>v n sume in May next. Whv should they obey the Legislature of New York, and not their own Legislature ? The position of New York is on all hands regretted. But how is it to be remedied? A single Legislature out of twenty-six Legislatures had passed a law forfeiting the charters of Banks, il they were unable to redeem their notes in specie. A public calamity overtakes the country and the declining pay specie, to so far from being criminal, became an act of public þÿsafety so adopted by all the Banks, and so confirmed by this very Legislature. The provision originally designed to guard against fraud, may thus become the punishment honesty of and ability. The Legislative body which protected the Banks for a year is now in session, and in twenty-four hours can extend the indemnity till a more appropriate season for resuming. I presume no difficulty will occur in tiiis. Why should there be? Is it possible that such a body can see with indifference the distress which a perseverance in this course must inevitably create, or permit tbe pride of opinion, or any mere political or party consideration to prevent them from interposing to protect their noble but sullering city ? If they decline how can we of Pennsylvania interfere ? Why should we voluntarily place ourselves in the same situation into which New York has been forced ? By doing so we share only a common disaster þÿ instead of husbanding our resources against the period when our interposition may be really useful. In the

mean while the most eflectual service which we can render, is to speak in a tone of sincerity. She may perhaps bear il from one, than w horn she fias never iiad a more true and constant friend þÿ who, although an entire stranger, has for a long series ol years done every tiling in Ins power to advance her prosperity, and never saw her in any misfortune, which he did not anxiously strive to mitigate, j But 1 wish to serve her. I believe then at this moment New York is in an entirely false to position. She is obliged by the existing law ; A five Stiver Loaf of fine Philadelphia Flour do what she feels to be wrong. Her natural course is to appeal to her representatives to rectify their mistake, and not to thrust out their own State Banks to bo governed by the Executive. Instead of doing this, she perseveres from a mistaken though honorable pride in not asking relief if attainable, but is preparing for the event by sacrificing her own interests and inflicting distress on the community. The apparent superiority in the exchanges which this produces is wholly fallacious as well as injurious The state of the exchanges in New York proves nothing whatever, except the seal city of money in New York. The exchanges are even less depreciated than many other tilings The bank notes of the Southern States are at a great depreciation. þÿ But store rent and real estate in the very spot where these notes are sacrificed, are much more depreciated than the notes themselves. So too in New York, the notes of Philadel-

phia are at a discount yet at this moment New York has to pay to Philadelphia little less than ten millions of dollars, for actual debts to Philadelphia, and to foreigners represented at Philadelphia. It is not therefore the abundance but the want of þÿmeans it is not strength but weakness which causes this difference. By the same process bread and meat may be reduced in price for tbe want
ty ol money, and then boast how much the little which remains will þÿbuy but your superiority is punished by thy debtor, who does

not settle with a creditoi so much above him. And what is the benefit of ail this. The other States are not obliged to submit to this local legislation, and the suflering of New York is certainly not fitted to make them adupt i' voluntarily. It is better therefore, for them to slate with perfect þÿl raikness that they do not mean to unite with her in this forced þÿresumption to say this decidedly and finally, so that she may apply the remedy þÿ an extension of her law. The whole subject would then he open for future adjustment upon principles of safety, alike to the Banks and the community. On the whole, the course which in my judgment, the Banks ought to pursue, is simply tins : The Banks should remain exactly as they are þÿ preparing to resume but not yet resuming. They should begin, as the Bank of England did, under similar circumstances, by paving the small notes, so as to restore coin to all minor channels of circulation-but not make any general resumption until they ascertain what course the Government will pursue, employing in tbe meantime their whole power to forward the crops to market. The American Banks should do in short what the American Army did at New Orleans, stand fast behind their cotton bales untill the enemy lias left the country. These are my opinions very deliberately formed, and very frankly expressed. They are thus set forth, not to influence the course of others, but to explain my own. With great respect and esteem, yours, N. BIDDLE. Philadelphia, April 5 1838

His Excellency the Governor General inspected and reviewed the Garrison and the different Corps of Christiansted' s Militia with that of the centre division on Saturday last; and on Tuesday, His Excellency reviewed tile Frederiksted' s Corps and Garrison ; the troops want through many evolutions and firings, and simulated attacks of positions, under the immediate command of His Excellency, who appeared much gratified with the good conduct and appearance of the different Corps. This is the first bloody sacrifice made by arbitrary power in Canada, of the lives of men, whose only crime is love of liberty. In the same ferocious spirit would every man who first moved in our revolutionary struggle, been exterminated, had Great Britain subdued them as she has the Canadian patriots. John Adams wrote on the Declaration of Independence to a feliow patriot þÿ þÿ posterity wdl rejoice, though you and I may rue þÿit. From the New York Evening Star. ARRIVAL OF THE STEAM SHIP SIRIUS FROM ( ORK l.N EIGHTEEN OATS. This vessel reached Sandy Hook last night and came up early this morning and anchored þÿoft the Battery, where she now lies. The announcement of this desired event flew like wildfire through the city, and crowds of persons from an early hour have been thronging to the Battery, and the small craft of the Whitehall boatmen have never had more active employment þÿ hundreds flocking oil in them to the great lion of our waters. We hastened down with the moving mass of population to the Battery, and soon saw the gallant steamers of the noble ship gleaming in the bright sunshine þÿ the star spangled banner at the foremast anit þÿBritannia s tandard hanging over the stern. Every body was struck with the noble bearing of this craft þÿ her ship like aspect, though longer than ordinary ships for the bulk and the neat rig of her masts. In fact she is a perfect sea boat. She is painted deep black, except the light green tatt'rail on the quarter and the gilding about the stern, and the paddles and shafts of the rim, and apparently delicate frame work of the wheels which are red and of iron, but nevertheless not in the slightest degree injured apparently, which to look at them seems astonishing, considering what billows the ship has waded through, and what heavy gales she lias encountered Neither s the roof of the roundhouse robbed apparently of a single plank. On arriving on board we were received

with great politeness by Lt. Richard Roberts, of her þÿMajesty navy, s commander of the ship. The vessel did not stop but one hour in the whole voyage, and that was on the Banks of Newfoundland during a heavy gale, and in order to fasten a screw. Never laid to once during the whole voyage. The þÿship company s is 49, exclusive of the Captain Lt. Richard Roberts, Royal Navy ; | Mr. Win. Ramsen, superintendent of the Engineers. First mate, John Dudley ; 2d do. George T. Briggs, 3d do. Francis S. Whitaker ; boatswain Richard Jones; first engi- j neer, John Lambert of Glasgow ; 2d do. Win. Dinner of Portsmouth ; fifteen firemen, 9 seamen þÿ The seamen all English, the firemen Irish, Scotch and English ; the rest are servants, stewards, &c. All the crew are British þÿ passengers 4G. Five ladies in first cabin from London and Cork, four in second cabin, a number of gentlemen, two schoolmasters, three artists, and several mechanics. During the whole course never shipped a sea ; never had the least apprehensions of any danger ; consumed 400 tons of Welch (bituminous) coal, and have a supply on hand ; never cleaned the boilers; the machinery worked beautifully during the gales, and Samuel þÿHall s condensers and improved engines, which were used, fully and completely sustained the high opinion entertained of them. No accident occurred. To Lieut Richard Roberts, therefore, belongs the honor ot having first achieved an experiment which it was easy to foresee was, from the extension to which coast steaming in
Europe and America had been previously carried, on the verge of consummation, but which it nevertheless required nerve and dicision to undertake, ilc appears perfectly

unconscious of the importance of the event which has been accomplished through his skill and courage. His own country will mark the event, and confer on the man some high honor, as we trust and believe. Gapt. Roberts is also commander of the largest steam packet ship afloat, viz. the British Queen (late Victoria) over 2000 tons, just completing at London, and from whence he sails in her on September next. The passage of the Sinus would have been at least 4 to G days less, but tor the heavy gales shortly after leaving Cork, and the constant westerly winds for' the first half of the voyage, with a dead, heavy, contused sea on, and especially during the two þÿdays severe weather on the Banks. The engine of the ship is entirely out of sight, and the pipe which is painted white, with a black top, and solid and broad, d- es not reach over some 20 feet above deck, standing as firm as when she left port. 'I lie wheel house does not come much below the gudgeon, leaving therefore the paddles arid the light iron frame work of spoke and rim, to which they are attached, open to sight. þÿ The paddles are each in form of a flight of three steps, each step narrow. London Begokrs þÿ In parts of Europe, particularly in London, begging is a regular vocation þÿ and it is pursued with a perseverance and an industry, which is hardly equalled in any other trade or profession þÿ and were not beggers an improvident people, they would soon grow rich þÿ and indeed many cases are cited of beggers in the streets of London, who have amassed large fortunes, by their economy and devoted attention to their business. A woman died a few years since in London, who had been a most indefatigable beggar in the vicinity of Charing Cross for twenty-five years, who left invested in good securities, property equal in value to £3000. In an association of beggars ©O to which she belonged, she was known by the name oi þÿ the þÿbanker, and was in the habit of lending small sums at an enormous rate of interest. Another case is related of a colored man, a miserable looking object, who labored industriously at the same vocation with astonishing success near Charing Cross for a number of years. After his death, on examining the wretched garret which he occupied, and which seemed the very emblem of poverty, the sum of £8000 in specie, was found snuglv deposited in divers old chests and boxes ! A wretched looking old woman, who exercised her honest calling on the Kent road, died not long since, and in her will left to a clerk in the Bunk of England, a legacy of fifteen hundred pounds sterling ! The reason assigned for this extraordinrry bequest, was that this gentleman put a penny into her hands
oftener than any other man in London ! The business has never yet been introduced into this country þÿ and probably never will. þÿ American Paper.

Sir. þÿ The Grampus has this moment returned from Vera Cruz, and brings the enclosed papers, being a report from Commander Breese, dated the 10th instant, and a copy of a letter to him, with circular enclosed from the French Commandant off Vera Cruz, declaring a blockade of all the ports of Mexico. The ultimatum and reply mentioned by Commander Breese was not forwarded by him, but I understand they, will be found in a package of papers from our Consul at Vera Cruz to the Secretary of State, which 1 this day transmit bv the regular mail. The Ontario and Concord are now in the Gulf þÿ the first at Vera Cruz and the latter oft' Tampico. The Vandalia sails to-morrow or next day for the coast of Texas and Mexico. 1 have the honor to be, very respectfully, your obedient servant, A. J. DALLAS. Hon. Maolon Dickerson, Secretary of the Navy, Washington, D. C.

Ship Ontario, 1 Sacrificios, April It!. 1838. $ Si >i þÿ 1 despatch the Grampus to apprise you that the French Minister, Baron DelT'audis, received yesterday from Mexico the reply of this Government to his ultimation, which not proving satisfactory, it has been determined to commence immediately the blockade of the ports of the Republic. Herewith 1 send the French commander's circular to that effect. I have requested our Consul to procure a copy of the French ultimatum, and the reply thereto, and hope to obtain them in time to forvvard by the schooner. There are no merchant vessels of any nation now in port, and but one American þÿ the Ann Elize, of New York þÿ expected. The blockade will be rigid as respects merchant vessels, but none others. The French force consists at present of one frigate and five brigs ; another frigate daily expected. A gun brig will leave this evening, with despatches for the French Minister in the United States, for Pensacola. The Concord is here, and 1 shall direct Captain Fitzhugh to proceed off Tainpioo, communicate with our Consul there, and proffer any assistance that our countrymen there may require at his hands. I shall remain with this ship here, until the excitement that the blockade may create on shore has subsided ; and then, if the presence of a vessel of war be no longer necessary, proceed to the coast of Texas in prosecution of your further orders. Very respectfully, sir, your obedient ser'vt. SAMUEL L. BREESE. Commodore A. J. Dallas, Commanding U. S.

The commander of the station of the Gulf of Mexico has the honor to inform Captain Breese, of the sloop of war Ontario, that he has just made known to the Mexican Government the blockade of all the ports of the Republic. He- sends enclosed a copy of the circular addressed by himself and the Minister

Plenipotentiary of France, to the French consuls established in Mexico ; and at the same time he begs Captain Breese to accept the assurance of his distinguished consideration. (Signed) BAZOCHE. Circular agreed upon between the Minister Plenipotentiary of France in Mexico, and the Commander of the Naval Station, notifying the French consuls established in Mexico of the declaration of the blockade of all the ports of the Republic. In consequence of the rejection of the ultimatum addressed on the 2ist of the last month to the Mexican Government, by order of the King Government, it has been determined that the ports of Mexico shall be immediately blockaded, lor the purpose of preventing all entry to our departure from them. In this state of tilings, the Baron Deftaudis and the Commander Buzoche have adopted the following principles for the blockade : 1. No neutral vessel proceeding towards the entrance of the blockaded ports shall be detained or captured, il' she lias not previously received from one of the vessels ol the 1'rench division a special notification of the existence of the blockade. 'J Ins notification shall be, moreover, inserted in wilting on the muster roll ol the neutral vissel, bv the cruiser which meeis her; and it shall contain the announcement, together with statements of the day and the laaiude in which ii was made. - Neutral vessels which may be already in one ol the ports of the Republic before the blockadt of sucli port, will have lr.il liberty to depart, with or without cargo, during fif-

teen days, dated from that upon which the blockade is established. 3. fhe ports of Vera Cruz and Tampico will remain entirely free for the entrance and departure of the British post office, militarv and non-commercial packet vessels. 4. Ine pons of tlie Mexican Republic shall remain entirely free for the entrance and dcpanurc ol Mexican boats exclusively engaged in fishing, unless the French naval division should be hereafter forced in retaliation, to withdraw this benevolent disposition. Translation of a note from the Miuisiur Plenipoteniiary of France, accompanied by a document fSut: I'he Mexican Government having þÿ j refused to accept the ultimatum, addressed, with the view ol efleciing a reconciliation, to j it, on the 21st of March last, by the French Government, the King's minister in Mexico, who is at this moment on board the fi igule l'tlerminie, has just communicated bv me, by means of the aimed brig I'Eelipse, sent for the purpose to l'ensacola, this refusal, as also the measures which it bad induced Captain Buzoelic, the commander ol ilie trench naval forces, to employ ; and 1 hasten, sir, agreeably to Ills Majesty s orders, to make known to the Government of the United States, the following official notification. All tiie ports of Mexico arc declared to be in a stale of blockade. 1 bis blockade is rendered eftective (or to be enforced) with regard to Vera Ciuz, from and alter the 1 5th of the last month and lias doubtless been since extended to the other ports of the Republic.

1 lie orders received by the commander, Lazoche, for the execution ol the dutv committed to him, are, as you see sir, from the annexed extract of the despatch sent to me bv Baron do Deffaudis, entirely conformable with the liberal principles professed by Fiance on the subjects ol blockades ; and they are

3U 'ttfcSJKIf J"-X- 81 drawn up in such a manner as to preserve neutrals, especially the vessels of the United Stales, from all restraints and vexations (entrayes) which are not absolutely indespensable for the attainment of the lawful ends proposed by the King's Government. On addressing you, sir, this communication, I have the honor to request that you would be so kind as to acknowledge the receipt of it as soon as possible, in order that the brig I'Eclipse may not be detained at Pensacola waiting for my answer longer than necessary. I avail myself, sir, of this occasion, to renew to you assurances of my high consideration. E. DE PONTOIS. To the Hon J. Forsith, Secretary of State of the United States.

We are indebted to the politeness of an attentive friend at Pittsburg, for slips containing the following particulars ofa most awful and destructive steamboat accident. From the Cincinnati Whig Extra. Cincinnati, April 25, 8 o'clock, 1\ ,17. Most Awful þÿSteam Bout Accident, Loss of I2.> Lives. It becomes again our painful dutv to record one of the most awful and destructive occurrences known in the terrible and fata catalogue of steam boat accidents. This afternoon about six o'clock, the new and elegant steam boat Moselle, Captain Perin, left the w harf of this city (full oi passengers) lor Louisville and Nt. Louis, and, with a view of taking a family onboard at Fulton about a inile arid a half above the quay, proceeded up the river, and made fast to a lumber raft for that purpose Icie the family were taken on board, and during the w hole time of the detention the Captain was holding on to all the steam he could create, with an intention of shewing off to the host advantage the great speed of tinboat as she passed down the whole length of the city. J he Moselle was a new brag boat, and had recently made several exceedingly quick trips to and from this place.

""JBm -fr Soon as the family were taken on board from the raft, the boat shoved oti ; and at the very moment her wheels made the first evolution, tier boilers burst with a most awful and astounding noise, equal to the most violent clap of thunder The explosion was destructive and heart-rending in the extreme, as we are assured by a gentleman who was sitting on his horse on the shore, waiting to see the boat start. ileads, limbs, bodies and blood, were Seen flying through the air in every direction, attended by the most horrible shrieks and groans from the wounded and the dying- The boat, at the moment of the accident, was about thirty feet from the shore, and was rendered a perfect wreck. She seemed to bo torn all to flinders as far back as the gentlemen' s cabin, and her hurricane deek (the whole length) was entirely swept away. The boat immediately began to sink rapidly, and float, with a strong current, down the river, at the same time getting farther from the shore. The Captain was thrown by the explosion entirely into the street, and was picked up dead and dreadfully mangled. Another man was thrown entirely through the roof of one of the neighboring houses, and limbs and fragments of bodies scattered about the river and shore in heart-rending profusion. Soon as the boat was discovered to be rapidly sinking, the passengers who remained unhurt in the gentlemen's anu Ladies' cabins, became panic st tuck, uiid with a fatuity unaccountable, jumped into the river. Being above the or-

dinary business parts of the city, there weie no boats at hand except a few large and unmanageable wood flats, which were carried to the relief of the sufferers as soon as possible, by a few persons on the shore. Many were drowned, however, before they could he rescued from a watery 'grave, and many sunk who were not seen afterwards. We are told that one little boy on shore was seen wringing his hands in agony, imploring those present to save his lather, mother, and three sisters, all of whom were struggling in the water to gain the shore, hut whom the poor little fellow had the awful misfortune to see perish, one by one, almost widen Ins reach. An infant child, belonging to this family, was picked up alive, floating down the river, on one of the fiagments of the hurricane deck. Doctor W ilson Hughes, ol the United Slates army, (and brother in-law to our estimable fellow citizen, VV. H.Hughes, of the l'earl street House,1 is doubtless among the slain, as he was known to have been on hoard, and some pieces of the military coat he had on, were picked up among the fragments. Mr Powell, a highly respectable grocery merchant in Louisville, and brother-in-law of Mr. Wilson Mc'Urew, of this city, is also supposed to be lost, lie was on hoard, and no tidings have since been heard of him, notw ithstanding the active inquiries of his friends. Wo arc unable, as yet, to particularize any other persons lost, sis the boat sunk in about fifteen minutes after the accident, leav-

ing nothing to he seen but her chimneys and a smud portion of her upper works, and also as a scene of distress and confusion iinuiediatcly ensued that altogether bailies description. Most ol the sufferers arc among the hands of the boat and the steerage passengers. It is supposed that there were about TWO HUNDRED PERSONS on hoard, of which number only from fifty to seventy-fiva are

XAWSK vaatmHuasst Miv \ va . xsooxmos AVJS. believed to have escaped, making the estimated loss of lives about ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE. Oh! tale of wo. The accident unquestionably occuried through sheer imprudence and carelessness '1 lie captain of the boat was desirous of showing off'lier great speed as she passed the city( and to overtake and pass another boat which had left tiie wharf for Louisville a short time before him. Dearly has he paid lor his silly ambition. The clerk ol the boat, we understand, escaped unhurt. These are all the particulars we have yet been able to learn, In to-morrow's Wiiig, we shall no doubt he able to give the names of many others who have been lost or killed.

STILL LATER. BY THIS EVENING'S MAIL. We have delayed our press beyond the usual lime to give the following additional particulars. Cincinnati, Thursday, 1 o'clock, P. M. We have just returned from the scene of horror occasioned by the explosion, and the account helore published, instead of being in the slightest degree exaggerated (us has been intimated by a lew,) falls far short of the dreadful reality. The fragments of human bodies are now laying scattered all along the shore, and we saw the corpses of a number so mangled and torn, that they hear scarcely any resemblance to the human form. We saw several with their heads and arms entirely blown off, others with only a part of the head destroyed, and others with their lower extremities shivered to an apparent jelley. Fragments of the boilers and other portions of the boat, were thrown from DO to 200 yards on tiie shore, some of them having passed entirely over the two rows of buildings on the street, and a portion of the boilers tearing away the gable end of a stable, situated high up the steep hill, in rear of the houses, at least 200 yards from the boat. It is positively stated that one man was picked up this morning on the Kentucky side, having been blown completely across the river. Only four bodies have to-day been taken from the boat, viz : a German woman and her two children, and another small boy. þÿ The number of dead and mangled bodies, altogether, that have been recovered, is about 20, as nearly as has yet been ascertained. A

number of persons, several wounded, have been sent to the hospital, but whose names we have not yet heard. The lower deck of the boat is yet entirely under water, and when the boat shall be raised a very large number ol persons, it is expected, will be found. There are no doubt more persons lost than wc have stated. We conversed, a while ago, with Mr. Broad well the agent of the boat, who says positively that there were 05 deck passengers, and 30 cabin passengers, whose names were entered on the boat's register, at l'ittsburg, Wheeling, and other towns on the river above this place, for Louisville, St Louis, and oilier places below. Here then are one hundred and thirty passengers that must have been on hoard, exclusive of the very large number who look passage at this place. The boat was unusually crowded, and Mr. Broadwell thinks the whole number on board, at the time of the accident, cannot be but little (if any) short of I HULL HUNDRED personal From the best information we can gather, it does not appear that more than thirty or forty of this number are known f» hare been rescued. L

is therefore orobable that tfie whole number drowned or destroyed, is some where in the neighbourhood of TWO HUNDHLD, OR TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY OR FORTY PERSONS! It is impossible that any accurate detail of the dead and missing can ever be made, or the precise number ascertained. A very large portion of them were deck passengers, whose humble sphere in life, will preclude the possibility of finding out their names.

Conflaoration. þÿ It is with feelings so harrowed that our pen almost drops from our hand in making the record, that we have to inscribe on our page this evening a conflagration that for its extent, its almost unutterable horrors and the accumulation of misfortunes it has heaped on our citizens, has had no parallel in the history of sjmilar afflictions to which our ill fated city has at various periods been devoted. þÿ Unfortunately a long period of draught, producing a scarcity of water and a more than usual portion of combustible material for the fire, gave it an intensity that spread over one fourth of our city with electrical rapidity. þÿ House after House, Square after Square were demolished, with a speed that seemed to concentrate all the worst horrors of a conflagration that defied contrivance and paralyzed energy in its extinguishments. We have never before witnessed a spectacle so awful, so harrowing, so heart sickening in all its direful accompaniments. þÿ The misfortune is almost irreparable, and is calculated to humble the pride of human ambition. It was but very recently that the citizens of Charleston were buoyant with hope, as to the improvement of its commercial fortunes and the increase of its population þÿ it is succeeded by despair þÿ by distress that knows 110 mitigation þÿ by calamity that cannot be described but may be imagined. But let us to our melancholy task. The alarm of fire was given between 8 and

0 o'clock last evening, the wind blowing fresh from the south west. Before the citizens assembled in adequate numbers to work the engines and the aparatus was providing for blowing up houses, sufficient time elapsed to envelope in flames the wooden two story house at the north west corner of King and Berresford streets, in the occupation of Mrs. Babson, and a small wooden tenement adjoining, occupied hv a fruiter, a free colored woman. It quickly communicated to the dwelling occupied by Mr. Simmons as a paint shop, on the opposite corner of Berresford and King street, but was arrested at the house in the occupation of Mr. Ladaveze, the 3d door from the S. W. corner of Berresford and King street. Streets running North anil South. On King street from the 2d door below Berresford street, all the houses are burnt on the Western side to Society street on the Eastern side from opposite Berresford to Society street. Beaufain street, all the houses on both sides to St Phillips street, Hassell street all the houses on both sides, including the Roman Catholic Chapel and the Hebrew Synagogue & the Methodist Church called Trinity, with the exception of the house on the North in the occupancy of John Stoney, Esq Wentworth street. While the conflagration was raging at its height a fresh alarm was given, and lire was found to proceed from a building called Norton's Mill, on Gadsden's wharf, which was burnt down, without however, doing other damage. The fire was arrested in all quarters at about 12 o'clock. M. having burned for 1.". hours, unremittingly. The amount insured 'in Charleston is about $1,200,000, of which it is supposed the offi ces here will be able to pay about 00 per cent þÿ a considerable amount on goods is insured in New York. But the most melancholy part of our duty remains to be performed, to wit, þÿ the record

of the death of valuable lives Among those who peiished from want of caution in blowing up houses, was Col. C. J Steedman, long known in our community as for his valuable qualities. Captain Dull, of the ship Herald, Messrs. Frederick Schnierle and J. S. Peirt. Among those seriously injured by explosions were Messrs. J. D. Brown and Mr. M. Torley. Messrs. Steedman and l'orley received their hurts wlnle blowing up a house on East Bay opposite Hassell street. Messrs Schnierle and .1 S. Peirt, while in the house at the corner of King and Liberty streets. þÿ Several blacks were killed from the same cause, one a black man who w as in the above house, and a mulatto boy named William belonging to Mrs Mitchell, who was literally blown to pieces It is a subject of lasting regret that buildings both public and private, which were ornamental or useful to the city, should have been involved in this wide spread destruction. Among these the New Hotel erected at an immense expense, is to be enumerated, and, what is a remarkable circumstance is that the new fire proof Stores lately built on Pearl street, were only slightly injured, while the buildings on every side of them were burnt The Roman Catholic Chapel anil Hebrew Synagogue were neat buildings, and among the private structures consumed, which the enterprise of their proprietors has lately erected, the large and elegant fire proof stores of Messrs. Mofl'et <Sz Calder, corner of Kir g and llassell streets, and those recently built by Messrs. Miller, Ripley & Co. were

most conspicuous. The Theatre narrowly escaped destruction, the cornices having taken fire. The flames were visible at 20 miles distance from the city. It is impossible to estimate the extent of the loss on any but important data. We think, however, that it cannot be less than
